title: 3  Feedstock on the Early Earth
section: 3.4 The early atmosphere: reducing or neutral?
text:
3.4 The early atmosphere: reducing or neutral?

Why the atmosphere matters
The composition of the early atmosphere determines which small organic molecules could be made in it. Experiments have shown that an electric discharge, acting on a mixture of water, methane and ammonia (or nitrogen), produces several biologically important organic compounds, including amino acids (Cleaves et al. 2008). Such experiments are discussed in Chapter 4. Their success depends strongly on the composition of the gas mixture, and this composition is the subject of this section.


Oxidation and reduction
The relevant property of the atmosphere is its oxidation state. Oxidation is the loss of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule; reduction is the gain of electrons. The two always occur together, in a redox reaction, because the electrons lost by one species are gained by another. For atoms in molecules, the bookkeeping is done with oxidation numbers: in a covalent bond, the shared electrons are assigned formally to the more electronegative atom (Section 2.4), and the oxidation number is the charge that each atom would carry if this assignment were real. Hydrogen is normally assigned +1 and oxygen −2.
With these rules, the carbon atom in methane (CH4) has oxidation number −4, in carbon monoxide (CO) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN) +2, and in carbon dioxide (CO2) +4. Nitrogen has −3 in ammonia (NH3) and 0 in N2 (Figure 3.6). An atmosphere is called reducing when carbon and nitrogen are present mainly in their low oxidation states, as CH4 and NH3, together with H2. It is called neutral (or weakly reducing) when they are present mainly as CO2 and N2, with water but without much H2 or free oxygen. The present atmosphere, which contains free O2, is oxidising.






Figure 3.6: Oxidation numbers of carbon and nitrogen in the gases discussed in this section. Moving to the right corresponds to oxidation (loss of electrons); moving to the left, to reduction. A reducing atmosphere contains the species on the left, a neutral atmosphere those on the right.





Gases from the interior
The earliest atmosphere was produced largely by the release of gases from the Earth’s interior. The elements available were hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and sulfur, and the molecules they form in volcanic gases depend on how oxidising the source magma is (Trail, Watson, and Tailby 2011). This is measured by the oxygen fugacity of the magma: the effective pressure of O2 in equilibrium with it, which is extremely small. Geologists describe it relative to reference buffers, assemblages of minerals that fix the oxygen fugacity at a known value at each temperature. Two buffers bracket the relevant range (Trail, Watson, and Tailby 2011):

the iron-wüstite buffer, defined by the coexistence of metallic iron and wüstite (FeO), which is strongly reducing;
the fayalite-magnetite-quartz buffer, defined by the coexistence of fayalite (Fe2SiO4), magnetite (Fe3O4) and quartz (SiO2), which corresponds to the oxidation state of present-day magmas.

The gases released under the two conditions are compared in Table 3.3.



Table 3.3: Volcanic gases expected from magmas of different oxidation state (Trail, Watson, and Tailby 2011).









Oxidation state of magma
Main volcanic gases




Near the iron-wüstite buffer (reducing)
CH4, H2, H2S, NH3, CO


Near the fayalite-magnetite-quartz buffer (present-day)
H2O, CO2, SO2, N2






Because the Hadean rock record is sparse or absent, the oxidation state of Hadean magmas has been estimated from zircons. Trail, Watson and Tailby used the amount of cerium incorporated into zircon crystals, which depends on the oxidation state of the melt, to estimate the oxygen fugacity of the melts from which Hadean zircons grew (Trail, Watson, and Tailby 2011). They found average values consistent with the fayalite-magnetite-quartz buffer, similar to present-day conditions, and values similar to those of present-day lavas from the mantle as early as about 4350 million years ago (Trail, Watson, and Tailby 2011). They concluded that gases released from the Earth’s interior later than about 200 million years after the formation of the solar system would not have produced a reducing atmosphere (Trail, Watson, and Tailby 2011).
This result agrees with the widely held view that the early atmosphere was not reducing but was dominated by N2 and CO2 (Cleaves et al. 2008). It is also consistent with the dense carbon dioxide atmosphere that followed the condensation of the oceans (Section 3.2).


Transient reducing atmospheres after impacts
A neutral atmosphere is less favourable for the synthesis of organic molecules than a reducing one. The action of electric discharges on neutral gas mixtures has been found to be much less efficient in producing organic compounds (Cleaves et al. 2008). This creates a problem: the origin of life has been argued to demand a highly reduced early atmosphere, rich in CH4, H2 and NH3, whereas the geological evidence suggests that the mantle has always been relatively oxidised and its gases dominated by CO2, H2O and N2 (K. J. Zahnle et al. 2020).
One proposed resolution involves the material that struck the Earth after the Moon-forming impact, called the late veneer (K. J. Zahnle et al. 2020). Isotopic evidence indicates that this material was extremely dry and highly reduced, and that it contained metallic iron (K. J. Zahnle et al. 2020). Zahnle and co-workers modelled what happens when such material reacts with the water of the oceans (K. J. Zahnle et al. 2020):

The main product of reaction between the iron of the impactor and the Earth’s water is H2.
The largest impacts, which vaporise the oceans, produce high pressures and long cooling times that favour the formation of CH4 and NH3. Smaller impacts are much less productive, unless catalysts were available or additional reducing power came from the Earth’s crust or mantle.
The resulting atmospheres rich in H2 and CH4 are transient. Through photochemistry, reactions driven by sunlight, they generate organic compounds containing nitrogen over periods of up to tens of millions of years, in total amounts that could form a layer up to half a kilometre thick, while hydrogen escapes to space.
When the methane has gone, the atmosphere is typically rich in H2 and CO, and is eventually oxidised to CO2.

In this picture the long-term state of the Hadean atmosphere was neutral, but it was interrupted by episodes, each lasting up to tens of millions of years, during which a reducing atmosphere could exist and organic molecules were produced efficiently.


Neutral atmospheres reconsidered
The yields of organic compounds from neutral atmospheres may also have been underestimated. Cleaves and co-workers repeated electric-discharge experiments with neutral gas mixtures and found that significant amounts of amino acids are produced (Cleaves et al. 2008). The low yields previously reported appear to have been caused by the destruction of the organic compounds, during the chemical treatment of the products, by nitrite and nitrate formed in the discharge. When an inhibitor of this oxidation, such as dissolved ferrous iron (Fe2+), was added, the yield of amino acids increased greatly (Cleaves et al. 2008). The authors concluded that synthesis in a neutral atmosphere may have depended on the availability of such oxidation inhibitors in the oceans, and may have been more important than previously thought (Cleaves et al. 2008).
The question of the composition of the early atmosphere is therefore not settled in a single answer. The evidence favours a long-term atmosphere of N2 and CO2, but leaves open the possibility of reducing conditions for limited times, or in limited places, which may have been enough for prebiotic chemistry.

title: 3  Feedstock on the Early Earth
text:
3.5 Sources of small molecules

Three categories of source
The small organic molecules from which the building blocks of RNA could be made had to come from somewhere. Chyba and Sagan divided the possible sources on the early Earth into three categories (Chyba and Sagan 1992):

Exogenous delivery: organic molecules already present in extraterrestrial objects, such as meteorites and interplanetary dust, and delivered intact to the Earth.
Impact-shock synthesis: organic molecules formed from simpler gases by the shock waves and heating produced when objects enter the atmosphere or strike the surface.
Endogenous synthesis by other energy sources: organic molecules formed on the Earth itself, using energy from ultraviolet light, electrical discharges such as lightning, or other sources.

To these may be added the chemistry of hydrothermal systems, in which water heated by contact with hot rock reacts with the rock and with dissolved gases.
Each category requires two things: a supply of carbon, nitrogen and other elements in a suitable chemical form, and a source of energy to drive reactions that would not otherwise proceed (Section 2.7). The relative importance of the categories therefore depends on the composition of the atmosphere discussed in Section 3.4.


Energy for atmospheric synthesis
Three energy sources can drive organic synthesis in the atmosphere.

Ultraviolet light is electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths shorter than those of visible light, that is, below about 400 nm. A photon of ultraviolet light carries enough energy to break chemical bonds; the energy of a photon is E = hc/\(\lambda\), where h = 6.626 070 15 × 10−34 J s is the Planck constant, c = 299 792 458 m s−1 the speed of light and \(\lambda\) the wavelength (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.a), so a photon of wavelength 200 nm has an energy of 6.2 eV, comparable to the bond enthalpies of Table 2.8 (a C–H bond enthalpy of 415.9 kJ mol−1 corresponds to 4.31 eV per bond). The fragments produced can then recombine to form new molecules. This is photochemistry (Section 3.4).
Electrical discharges, such as lightning, heat a narrow channel of gas to high temperatures and break molecules into atoms, ions and fragments, which recombine as the gas cools.
Shocks from objects entering the atmosphere at high speed heat and compress gas in a similar way.

Chyba and Sagan estimated the amount of organic material produced by each source for different compositions of the early atmosphere (Chyba and Sagan 1992). Their main conclusions were:

In a strongly reducing atmosphere, production by atmospheric shocks seems to have exceeded that by electrical discharges. Production by ultraviolet light may have exceeded both, but only if a gas such as H2S, which absorbs ultraviolet light of long wavelength, was supplied fast enough (Chyba and Sagan 1992).
In an atmosphere of intermediate oxidation state, which they considered more likely, shocks were probably of little importance. For a ratio of H2 to CO2 of about 0.1, the net production of organic molecules was some three orders of magnitude (a factor of about 1000) lower than for reducing atmospheres; the most important sources were ultraviolet light and the delivery of intact organic molecules in interplanetary dust particles (Chyba and Sagan 1992).
At still lower ratios of H2 to CO2, interplanetary dust particles may have been the dominant source (Chyba and Sagan 1992).

The general conclusion is that the more oxidised the atmosphere, the less organic material it produces, and the more important delivery from space becomes. Endogenous, exogenous and impact-shock sources could each have contributed significantly to the origin of life (Chyba and Sagan 1992).


Delivery from space
Interplanetary dust particles (IDPs) are small particles of extraterrestrial dust that fall on the Earth from space; Chyba and Sagan considered them the most likely carrier of intact organic molecules from space (Chyba and Sagan 1992). Meteorites are larger bodies that survive passage through the atmosphere and reach the ground. Some meteorites contain a remarkable variety of organic compounds. An analysis of the organic fraction of the Murchison meteorite (Section 3.7) found tens of thousands of different molecular compositions, corresponding to probably millions of different structures (Schmitt-Kopplin et al. 2010).
Meteorites and interplanetary dust also delivered molecules of biological interest, including nucleobases (Pearce et al. 2017), the components of nucleotides that carry genetic information (Chapter 5). Pearce and co-workers modelled the fate of meteoritic nucleobases delivered into small ponds that were repeatedly filled with water and dried (Pearce et al. 2017). In their model the nucleobases came mainly from meteorites rather than from interplanetary dust particles, and were quickly lost, by seepage of water out of the ponds during wet periods and by destruction by ultraviolet light during dry periods (Pearce et al. 2017). Any chemistry that used them must therefore have been fast. The model is discussed further in Section 3.7.


Impacts as sources of reducing power
Impacts can also change the chemistry of the atmosphere as a whole. As described in Section 3.4, the impact of large bodies containing metallic iron on an ocean-covered Earth may have produced transient atmospheres rich in H2 and CH4, in which nitrogen-containing organic compounds were generated photochemically over periods of up to tens of millions of years (K. J. Zahnle et al. 2020). In this picture impacts do not merely deliver or synthesise organic molecules directly; they also supply the reducing conditions that make atmospheric synthesis efficient.


Hydrothermal systems
Hydrothermal vents are sites on the sea floor where water heated within the crust flows out into the ocean. They are geochemically reactive environments, and today they support rich communities of microorganisms (Martin et al. 2008). Hydrothermal fluids contain hydrogen (H2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) (Martin et al. 2008), which form a redox couple: a reducing and an oxidising substance that can react with each other by the transfer of electrons. There are striking parallels between the chemistry of this couple and the central energy-yielding reactions of some modern microorganisms that make their organic matter from CO2 (autotrophs) (Martin et al. 2008). This has led to the proposal that the chemistry of life began in such settings (Martin et al. 2008).
Hydrothermal systems therefore offer an endogenous source of reduced carbon that does not depend on the composition of the atmosphere. Their limitations for the synthesis of RNA, in particular the instability of RNA and its components in hot water, are discussed in later chapters.


Feedstock and energy in one system
The categories above are not exclusive. One influential set of experiments by Patel and co-workers showed that precursors of ribonucleotides (the units of RNA), amino acids and lipids can all be made from hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and some of its derivatives, by a sequence of reactions in which ultraviolet light provides energy and hydrogen sulfide (H2S) acts as the reducing agent (Patel et al. 2015). Such chemistry combines an atmospheric or exogenous source of carbon and nitrogen (HCN), a geochemical source of reducing power (H2S), and sunlight. The key molecules of this and other routes are introduced in Section 3.6.
Figure 3.7 summarises the sources described in this section.






Figure 3.7: Sources of small organic molecules on the early Earth, following the three categories of Chyba and Sagan (1992), with hydrothermal systems added (Martin et al. 2008). Arrows show the flow of material to the surface environment in which prebiotic chemistry may have taken place. The relative importance of the sources depends on the oxidation state of the atmosphere.

title: 3  Feedstock on the Early Earth
text:
3.6 Key feedstock molecules

What is a feedstock molecule?
A feedstock molecule is a small, simple molecule from which more complex molecules can be built in a sequence of reactions. In prebiotic chemistry the term refers to molecules that could plausibly have formed or accumulated on the early Earth by the processes of Section 3.5, and that react, under suitable conditions, to give the building blocks of biological molecules. This section introduces four of them: hydrogen cyanide, formaldehyde, cyanamide and phosphate, together with the phosphorus mineral schreibersite. How they are converted into the building blocks of RNA is the subject of Chapters 4 and 5.
The first three are compounds of hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen. Their structures and some of their properties are given in Figure 3.8 and Table 3.4.

Figure 3.8: Structures of the feedstock molecules discussed in this section. Lines represent covalent bonds (Section 2.2); double and triple bonds are drawn as two and three lines. Hydrogen cyanide is linear and contains a carbon-nitrogen triple bond; formaldehyde is planar and contains a carbon-oxygen double bond; cyanamide contains an amino group (NH2) bonded to a nitrile group (C\(\equiv\)N). The phosphate ion is tetrahedral (drawn here in projection); its charge of −3 is spread over the four oxygen atoms.





Hydrogen cyanide
Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) is a linear molecule in which the carbon atom forms a single bond to hydrogen and a triple bond to nitrogen (Section 2.3). It boils at 299.0 K (25.9 °C) (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.b), so on a warm early Earth it could exist as a gas in the atmosphere and dissolve in water. In the classification of Section 3.4, its carbon atom has oxidation number +2, intermediate between that of methane and that of carbon dioxide. In the transient reducing atmospheres that may have followed large impacts, nitrogen-containing organic compounds are generated photochemically (K. J. Zahnle et al. 2020); HCN is the simplest compound of this kind.
HCN is of central importance because it contains carbon and nitrogen bonded together, as they are in the nucleobases of RNA. Concentrated solutions of ammonium cyanide (NH4CN), the salt formed from HCN and ammonia, polymerise. The products include the nucleobases adenine and guanine; this chemistry goes back to original studies by Oró and Kimball in 1961 and has been examined in later work (Borquez et al. 2005). The yields are low: about 0.1 percent of adenine after hydrolysis of the soluble products at pH 8, and about 0.05 percent from the insoluble black polymer that also forms (Borquez et al. 2005). Adenine has the molecular formula C5H5N5, which is exactly five times that of HCN; the chemistry of this and related reactions is described in Chapter 5.
HCN is also the starting point of the reaction network of Patel and co-workers described in Section 3.5, from which precursors of ribonucleotides, amino acids and lipids can all be derived (Patel et al. 2015).


Formaldehyde
Formaldehyde (H2CO) is the simplest aldehyde, a compound containing the group –CHO, in which a carbon atom is double-bonded to oxygen and bonded to hydrogen. It is planar, with an sp2-hybridised carbon atom (Section 2.3), and boils at 253.85 K (−19.3 °C) (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.b).
Formaldehyde is the feedstock for sugars. In 1861 Butlerov discovered that formaldehyde, treated with a base, is converted into a sugary substance (Boutlerow 1861); the process is now called the formose reaction. In 1959 Breslow proposed a mechanism in which glycolaldehyde, the simplest molecule formed from two formaldehyde units, catalyses its own formation, so that the reaction is autocatalytic (Section 2.8) (Breslow 1959). The sugar of RNA, ribose, contains five carbon atoms and can in principle be formed from five formaldehyde units. In practice, however, ribose is difficult to form selectively (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009), and the formose reaction gives a complex mixture. This problem is examined in Section 4.4.


Cyanamide
Cyanamide (H2NCN) consists of an amino group, –NH2, bonded to a nitrile group, –C\(\equiv\)N. In the solid state it melts near its triple-point temperature of 318.71 K (45.56 °C) (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.b).
Its importance in prebiotic chemistry was shown in 2009 by Powner, Gerland and Sutherland (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009). They synthesised activated pyrimidine ribonucleotides, two of the four units from which RNA is built, by a short sequence of reactions that does not pass through free ribose or free nucleobases (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009). The starting materials were cyanamide, cyanoacetylene (HC\(\equiv\)C–C\(\equiv\)N), glycolaldehyde, glyceraldehyde and inorganic phosphate, all regarded as plausible prebiotic feedstock molecules (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009). This synthesis is described in detail in Chapter 5.


Phosphate and the phosphate problem
Every nucleotide of RNA contains a phosphate group, so a source of phosphorus in a reactive form is essential. At the Earth’s surface phosphorus occurs mainly as phosphate, PO43−, an ion in which a phosphorus atom (oxidation number +5) is bonded tetrahedrally to four oxygen atoms. Phosphate is also a component of cell membranes and of energy-transfer molecules such as adenosine triphosphate (ATP) (Toner and Catling 2020).
Two obstacles make phosphate difficult to use in prebiotic chemistry. First, phosphorus is scarce in the crust: phosphorus pentoxide (P2O5) makes up only 0.15 percent of the upper continental crust by mass (Table 1.3). Second, phosphate combines with calcium to form minerals of the apatite group, which have low solubility. As a result, dissolved phosphate is generally limited to micromolar concentrations in natural waters, whereas laboratory experiments that attach phosphate to organic molecules commonly use molar concentrations, about a million times higher (Toner and Catling 2020). This mismatch between laboratory conditions and environmental constraints is known as the phosphate problem (Toner and Catling 2020).
Concentrations here are expressed in moles of solute per litre of solution (molar, symbol M) or per kilogram of solvent (molal, symbol mol kg−1); for dilute aqueous solutions the two are nearly equal.
Two proposed solutions illustrate the kinds of setting that may have overcome the phosphate problem.

Carbonate-rich lakes. In lakes rich in dissolved carbonate, calcium is removed from solution as carbonate minerals, so phosphate does not precipitate as apatite. Toner and Catling calculated that such lakes could accumulate up to about 0.1 molal phosphate under steady evaporation and inflow, and more than 1 molal during evaporation without inflow, at moderate pH (6.5 to 9) buffered by the CO2-rich atmosphere (Toner and Catling 2020). Before the origin of life there were no microorganisms to consume phosphate, which would have made such lakes even richer in it (Toner and Catling 2020).
Reduced phosphorus from meteorites. Iron meteorites contain schreibersite, (Fe,Ni)3P, a mineral in which phosphorus is bonded to iron and nickel rather than to oxygen. When schreibersite corrodes in water, it releases a mixture of phosphorus-bearing ions, including pyrophosphate and triphosphate (chains of two and three phosphate units) and phosphonate, in which phosphorus is less oxidised than in phosphate (Pasek and Lauretta 2005). Iron meteorites were therefore probably an important source of reactive phosphorus (Pasek and Lauretta 2005). Gull and co-workers showed that synthetic schreibersite, simply mixed with aqueous solutions of the nucleosides adenosine or uridine and mildly heated under slightly basic conditions (pH about 9), attaches phosphate groups to them (Gull et al. 2015). (A nucleoside is a nucleobase joined to ribose; adding a phosphate gives a nucleotide; see Chapter 5.)

Neither solution is established. Both show, however, that the availability of phosphate depended on local conditions, a point taken up in Section 3.7.

title: 3  Feedstock on the Early Earth
text:
3.7 Candidate settings

Requirements of a setting
The preceding sections described where small molecules could come from. Prebiotic chemistry, however, also requires a place where these molecules could accumulate and react. A useful setting must bring feedstock molecules together at concentrations high enough for reactions between them to proceed, supply energy, and protect the products long enough for further steps to occur. Different settings meet these requirements in different ways. Four kinds of setting have been proposed: ponds and hot springs on land, hydrothermal vents on the sea floor, impact craters, and ice. Each is described below, and their main features are compared in Table 3.5.
Before turning to the settings, it is worth recalling the evidence for the earliest delivery of organic matter from space, since it bears on all of them.






TipKey experiment: organic molecules in the Murchison meteorite



On 28 September 1969, a meteorite fell near the town of Murchison, Victoria, Australia (Meteoritical Society 2026). It is a carbonaceous chondrite, a chondrite (Section 1.7) rich in carbon, of the group designated CM2, and about 100 kg of material was recovered (Meteoritical Society 2026).
In 1970 Kvenvolden and co-workers reported evidence for extraterrestrial amino acids and hydrocarbons in the Murchison meteorite (Kvenvolden et al. 1970). Later work extended the list to many other classes of compound. Callahan and co-workers analysed 12 meteorites and found that Murchison and one other meteorite contained a diverse suite of nucleobases, including three nucleobase analogues that are rare on Earth: purine, 2,6-diaminopurine and 6,8-diaminopurine (Callahan et al. 2011). These compounds were not detected in control samples, including a terrestrial soil and Antarctic ice, which supports their extraterrestrial origin (Callahan et al. 2011). The same suite of nucleobases was produced in laboratory reactions of ammonium cyanide, suggesting that the meteoritic purines formed by cyanide chemistry on the meteorite’s parent asteroid (Callahan et al. 2011) (Section 3.6).
A non-targeted analysis of the material that can be extracted from Murchison with solvents found tens of thousands of different molecular compositions, corresponding to probably millions of distinct structures (Schmitt-Kopplin et al. 2010). The Murchison meteorite thus shows that chemistry producing some of the molecules of interest to the origin of life took place on small bodies of the early solar system, independently of the Earth, and that its products reached the Earth’s surface.




Ponds and hot springs on land
Small bodies of water on land, from shallow ponds to the pools of volcanic hot springs, can dry out and refill repeatedly. These wet-dry cycles are their most important feature: they have been found to promote the joining of building blocks into chains (Pearce et al. 2017; Damer and Deamer 2020). During the dry phase dissolved molecules are concentrated, and during the wet phase products are redistributed and new material is supplied. Damer and Deamer have developed a hypothesis in which fluctuating volcanic hot-spring pools play a central role, based on experimental evidence that polymers enclosed in lipid membranes can be synthesised by cycles of hydration and dehydration (Damer and Deamer 2020).
The model of Pearce and co-workers, introduced in Section 3.5, placed meteoritic nucleobases in such ponds (Pearce et al. 2017). Ponds could exist only once land had risen above the early global ocean, but the growing area of land was offset by a declining rate of meteorite delivery (Pearce et al. 2017). Because nucleobases were lost rapidly by seepage and by ultraviolet light, the authors concluded that the formation of nucleotides and their joining into RNA must have occurred within one to a few wet-dry cycles, and that, under these conditions, RNA polymers probably appeared before 4.17 billion years ago (Pearce et al. 2017).
The carbonate-rich lakes of Section 3.6 are a related setting: closed basins in which evaporation concentrates phosphate and other reagents to levels used in laboratory syntheses (Toner and Catling 2020). Surface settings are exposed to ultraviolet light, which can drive reactions such as those of Patel et al. (2015) but can also destroy their products.


Hydrothermal vents
Hydrothermal vents (Section 3.5) place chemistry in the deep ocean, protected from ultraviolet light and from the effects of all but the largest impacts. Many vents, such as the black smokers of mid-ocean ridges, are driven by volcanic heat (Kelley et al. 2005). A different type is represented by the Lost City hydrothermal field, which is not volcanically driven (Kelley et al. 2005). There, reactions between seawater and rocks of the upper mantle produce fluids rich in methane and hydrogen, at temperatures from below 40 °C to 90 °C and at pH 9 to 11, and the fluids build carbonate chimneys 30 to 60 metres tall (Kelley et al. 2005).
Alkaline vents of this kind provide H2, a strong reducing agent, in contact with seawater that contained CO2. The parallels between this H2-CO2 chemistry and the core energy metabolism of some microorganisms (Section 3.5) underlie the proposal that life began in such vents (Martin et al. 2008). A difficulty for the synthesis of RNA in the open ocean is dilution: molecules that are formed disperse into a very large volume of water unless they are retained, for example within the porous interiors of chimneys.


Impact craters
Impacts were not only destructive. Osinski and co-workers reviewed the ways in which impacts may have assisted the origin of life (Osinski et al. 2020). The heat deposited by a large impact can drive hydrothermal systems within the crater, on land or beneath the sea, which may persist long after the impact; impacts also create sediment-filled basins and pools, and they can deliver or generate chemical ingredients for life and mineral surfaces such as clays that can act as catalysts (Osinski et al. 2020). An impact crater can thus combine several of the features of the other settings in one place. As noted in Section 3.4, large impacts of iron-rich bodies may in addition have produced transient reducing atmospheres (K. J. Zahnle et al. 2020).


Ice
Low temperatures slow down reactions (Section 2.8), but they also slow down the decomposition of products, and freezing can concentrate solutes: as water freezes, dissolved substances are largely excluded from the growing ice crystals and accumulate in the remaining liquid. Levy and co-workers kept dilute solutions of ammonium cyanide frozen for 25 years at −20 °C and −78 °C (Levy et al. 2000). Adenine and guanine, together with a simple set of amino acids dominated by glycine, were formed in substantial yields (Levy et al. 2000). Cold settings may therefore have been suitable for some prebiotic syntheses, and may have been common if the faint young Sun (Section 3.2) left parts of the early Earth frozen.


Comparison



Table 3.5: Candidate settings for prebiotic chemistry on the early Earth.











Setting
Main advantages
Main difficulties
Key evidence




Ponds and hot springs on land
Wet-dry cycles concentrate molecules and favour joining of building blocks; access to ultraviolet light
Require exposed land; ultraviolet light also destroys products
Damer and Deamer (2020), Pearce et al. (2017), Toner and Catling (2020)


Hydrothermal vents
Continuous supply of H2 and chemical energy; protection from ultraviolet light and most impacts
Dilution in the ocean; high temperatures in some vents
Martin et al. (2008), Kelley et al. (2005)


Impact craters
Combine heat, hydrothermal circulation, pools and delivered material
Each event is local and its hydrothermal activity eventually ceases
Osinski et al. (2020)


Ice
Slow decomposition; concentration of solutes on freezing
Slow reactions
Levy et al. (2000)






No single setting has been shown to be the one in which life began, and several may have contributed different steps. What the evidence of this chapter establishes is that, by about 4.4 Ga, the Earth had liquid water (Section 3.3), that its atmosphere was probably neutral for most of the time but may have been reducing for periods after large impacts (Section 3.4), and that organic molecules, including nucleobases, were supplied from both terrestrial and extraterrestrial sources (Section 3.5). The next chapter follows the chemistry by which feedstock molecules such as those of Section 3.6 are transformed into the building blocks of life.

title: 3  Feedstock on the Early Earth
text:
Summary

Radioactive decay follows N = N0 e−\(\lambda t\), with half-life t1/2 = ln 2/\(\lambda\). The ratio of radiogenic daughter to remaining parent in a closed system gives the time since the system closed.
The uranium-lead system provides two independent clocks with half-lives of 4.4683 Ga and 703.81 Ma; their agreement tests whether a sample has remained closed. Lead-lead ages date the oldest solids of the solar system to 4.567 to 4.568 Ga.
Patterson’s meteorite lead measurements of 1956 gave an age of 4.55 ± 0.07 Ga for the Earth and meteorites, close to the modern age of the oldest solar-system solids.
Earth history is divided into four eons; the Hadean ends at 4031 ± 3 Ma and the Archean at 2500 Ma.
The Moon formed when a Mars-sized body struck the proto-Earth. Zircons from Apollo 14 show that the Moon had solidified by 4.51 Ga, so the impact occurred within about 60 million years of the formation of the solar system.
After the impact the Earth passed through a silicate-vapour atmosphere and a magma ocean lasting about 2 million years; water then condensed into oceans beneath a dense carbon dioxide atmosphere. Habitable conditions may have been reached 10 to 20 million years after the impact.
The young Sun was about 30 percent fainter than today, so the early Earth needed more greenhouse gases to keep liquid water. Impacts continued throughout the Hadean, with an episode of elevated impact rate between about 4.2 to 4.0 and 3.5 Ga.
Detrital zircons from the Jack Hills, Western Australia, are up to 4404 ± 8 million years old. Their high \(\delta\)18O values show that by 4.4 Ga surface rocks had interacted with liquid water: the Earth had oceans early in the Hadean.
Graphite inclusions in a 4.10 Ga zircon have \(\delta\)13C = −24 ± 5 ‰, consistent with, but not proof of, a biological origin.
In a reducing atmosphere carbon and nitrogen are present mainly as CH4 and NH3; in a neutral one, as CO2 and N2. Cerium in Hadean zircons indicates that magmas were as oxidised as today’s, so gases from the interior would have formed a neutral atmosphere.
Transient reducing atmospheres, lasting up to tens of millions of years, may have followed large impacts of iron-bearing material, and organic synthesis in neutral atmospheres may be more efficient than once thought.
Organic molecules could be delivered from space, made by impact shocks, or made on the Earth by ultraviolet light and electrical discharges; hydrothermal systems provide a further source. The more oxidised the atmosphere, the smaller the atmospheric production and the more important delivery from space.
Key feedstock molecules include hydrogen cyanide (a source of nucleobases), formaldehyde (a source of sugars through the formose reaction) and cyanamide. Phosphate is scarce and poorly soluble in the presence of calcium (the phosphate problem); carbonate-rich lakes and the meteoritic mineral schreibersite are two proposed sources of usable phosphorus.
The Murchison meteorite, which fell in 1969, contains amino acids, a diverse suite of nucleobases and tens of thousands of other organic compounds of extraterrestrial origin.
Proposed settings for prebiotic chemistry include ponds and hot springs on land (wet-dry cycles), hydrothermal vents, impact craters and ice. Each offers advantages and difficulties, and none has been established as the site of the origin of life.

Exercises

Show, starting from Equation 3.2, that the half-life equals ln 2/\(\lambda\). Calculate the decay constant of potassium-40 from its half-life in Table 3.1.
A zircon crystal has a radiogenic 206Pb/238U atom ratio of 0.70. Using Equation 3.5, calculate its 238U-206Pb age.
What fraction of the potassium-40 present when the solar system formed remains today? Of the potassium-40 that has decayed, what fraction has become argon-40?
Explain why carbon-14 cannot be used to date rocks from the Hadean eon.
A uranium-bearing mineral gives a 238U-206Pb age of 3.9 Ga and a 235U-207Pb age of 4.1 Ga. Is it concordant? Which assumption of Equation 3.5 has probably failed?
Explain why lead from the troilite of the Canyon Diablo meteorite was important for Patterson’s determination of the age of the Earth.
Using the data in Section 3.2, calculate the mean density of the Moon from its mass and radius, and compare your result with the tabulated value.
What does the similarity of the oxygen isotope compositions of the Earth and Moon imply about the giant impact?
Why is the age of 4.51 Ga obtained from lunar zircons a minimum age for the Moon-forming impact?
Using Equation 3.6, calculate the luminosity of the Sun, relative to its present value, at 3.8 Ga.
List the stages through which the surface of the Earth passed between the giant impact and the first oceans, with the approximate duration of each.
A zircon has an 18O/16O ratio 0.74 percent higher than that of VSMOW. What is its \(\delta\)18O value?
Explain why a detrital zircon can be much older than the sedimentary rock in which it is found.
Explain the reasoning by which a high \(\delta\)18O value in a zircon is taken as evidence for liquid water at the Earth’s surface.
Why should the graphite in the 4.10 Ga Jack Hills zircon be regarded as potentially, rather than certainly, biological in origin?
Assign oxidation numbers to each atom in H2O, NH3, HCN and CO2.
Write a balanced equation for the reaction of metallic iron with water to give wüstite (FeO) and hydrogen. Which element is oxidised and which is reduced?
Explain why the oxidation state of Hadean magmas determines the composition of the gases they release.
Why are the reducing atmospheres proposed by Zahnle and co-workers described as transient?
Calculate the energy, in eV, of a photon of wavelength 250 nm. Is it sufficient to break an O–H bond (Table 2.8)?
According to Chyba and Sagan, which sources of organic molecules were most important in an atmosphere with [H2]/[CO2] of about 0.1? Explain why the answer differs for a strongly reducing atmosphere.
Explain why the nucleobases delivered to a pond by a meteorite could have been used only in chemistry that was completed within a short time.
What is a redox couple? Identify the oxidising and the reducing member of the couple H2-CO2.
Assign oxidation numbers to every atom in formaldehyde and in cyanamide.
Show that the molecular formula of adenine, C5H5N5, corresponds to five molecules of HCN. Do the same for ribose, C5H10O5, and formaldehyde.
A laboratory experiment uses 1 M phosphate, and a natural water contains 2 \(\mu\)M phosphate. By what factor do the concentrations differ?
Explain why carbonate-rich lakes can contain much more dissolved phosphate than ordinary natural waters.
What evidence indicates that the nucleobases found in the Murchison meteorite are extraterrestrial rather than terrestrial contamination?
Explain how wet-dry cycles can help to overcome the problem of low concentrations of feedstock molecules.
Compare a land-based hot-spring pool with an alkaline hydrothermal vent as a setting for prebiotic chemistry, considering energy sources, concentration of molecules and exposure to ultraviolet light.
Why might freezing promote some prebiotic reactions even though low temperature reduces rate constants?

title: 4  From Simple Molecules to Building Blocks
text:
4.1 Functional groups

Skeletons and functional groups
The molecules of Chapter 3 contain at most a few atoms. The building blocks of RNA are larger: the sugar ribose has 20 atoms and the nucleobase adenine 15. To describe such molecules, chemists divide them into parts. An organic molecule is regarded as consisting of a relatively unreactive skeleton, for example a chain of carbon atoms joined by single bonds, to which one or more functional groups are attached. A functional group is an atom, or a group of atoms, that has similar chemical properties whenever it occurs in different compounds, and it determines the characteristic physical and chemical properties of the family of compounds that contain it (IUPAC, n.d.h).
This division is useful because the reactions of a molecule are, to a good approximation, the reactions of its functional groups. Once the behaviour of a few functional groups is known, the behaviour of a large number of molecules can be predicted. In what follows, the letter R stands for the rest of the molecule, a carbon-containing group whose details do not matter for the reaction under discussion.


The functional groups of this book
Table 4.1 lists the functional groups that occur in the building blocks of RNA and in their precursors. Their structures are shown in Figure 4.1.

Figure 4.1: Structures of the functional groups of Table 4.1. R and R\('\) represent the rest of the molecule. The carbonyl group, a carbon atom double-bonded to an oxygen atom, is common to aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, amides and carboxylic esters.



The groups are described below.

Alcohols are compounds in which a hydroxy group, –OH, is attached to a carbon atom that forms only single bonds (IUPAC, n.d.a). The O–H bond is polar (Section 2.4), so hydroxy groups form hydrogen bonds with water and with one another (Section 2.5). Ribose carries several hydroxy groups, which is why it dissolves readily in water.
The carbonyl group consists of a carbon atom double-bonded to an oxygen atom, C=O. Because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, the carbon atom carries a partial positive charge, and this is the site at which carbonyl compounds react with electron-rich species. In an aldehyde, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to one hydrogen atom and to one R group, RC(=O)H (IUPAC, n.d.b); formaldehyde, H2CO, is the special case in which R is a second hydrogen atom. In a ketone, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon atoms.
A carboxylic acid contains the carboxy group, –COOH, in which a carbonyl group and a hydroxy group are attached to the same carbon atom. The hydrogen of the hydroxy group can be released as H+ in water (Section 2.6), leaving the carboxylate ion –COO−.
An amine contains a nitrogen atom bonded to one or more carbon atoms and carrying a lone pair (Section 2.2); the simplest form is the amino group, –NH2. The lone pair can accept a proton, so amines are bases.
An amide is formally derived from an acid by replacing a hydroxy group of the acid with an amino or substituted amino group (IUPAC, n.d.c). In a carboxylic amide, the carbonyl group is therefore bonded directly to nitrogen, –CO–NH2. Formamide, HCONH2, the simplest amide, is a starting material for the synthesis of nucleobases (Section 4.5).
A nitrile contains a carbon atom triple-bonded to nitrogen, –C\(\equiv\)N, the group present in HCN and cyanamide (Section 3.6).
An ester is formally derived from an acid and an alcohol by linking them with the loss of water, from a hydroxy group of the acid and the hydroxy group of the alcohol (IUPAC, n.d.g). The acid need not be a carboxylic acid: phosphoric acid forms phosphate esters, and it is through phosphate ester linkages that the units of RNA are joined into a chain (Chapter 6).



Isomers
Molecules with the same molecular formula can have different structures. Isomers are species that have the same atomic composition (molecular formula) but different arrangements of their atoms, and hence different physical or chemical properties (IUPAC, n.d.i). For example, glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone both have the formula C3H6O3. In glyceraldehyde the carbonyl group is at the end of the carbon chain, so the molecule is an aldehyde; in dihydroxyacetone it is in the middle, so the molecule is a ketone (Figure 4.2). Isomers of this kind, which differ in the order in which atoms are bonded, are called structural isomers.
Ribose has the formula C5H10O5, and many other sugars share this formula. The problem of forming ribose rather than one of its isomers is central to Section 4.4.


Chirality
A second kind of isomerism arises from the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms. An object is chiral if it cannot be superposed on its mirror image (IUPAC, n.d.d). In molecules, chirality most often arises from a carbon atom bonded to four different groups. Such a carbon atom is called a stereocentre. Because the four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron (Section 2.3), the four groups can be arranged in two ways that are mirror images of each other and cannot be interconverted without breaking bonds (Figure 4.2).
Two molecules that are non-superposable mirror images of each other are called enantiomers. Enantiomers have identical physical properties, such as melting point and solubility, except in their interaction with other chiral objects, including polarised light and other chiral molecules. Glyceraldehyde has one stereocentre, its central carbon atom, and therefore exists as two enantiomers, designated D and L. Ribose has three stereocentres in its open-chain form, and the ribose in RNA is exclusively D-ribose. A chemical synthesis from achiral starting materials such as formaldehyde gives equal amounts of the two enantiomers, a mixture called a racemate. How the uniform chirality of biological molecules arose is one of the open questions discussed in Section 4.7.






Figure 4.2: Isomers of C3H6O3. Top: the structural isomers glyceraldehyde (an aldehyde) and dihydroxyacetone (a ketone). Bottom: the two enantiomers of glyceraldehyde, D and L, drawn as mirror images about their stereocentre (marked with an asterisk). The enantiomers are drawn so that the horizontal bonds (wedges) point towards the viewer and the vertical bonds (dashed) away from the viewer; in this orientation the hydroxy group of D-glyceraldehyde lies on the right.

title: 4  From Simple Molecules to Building Blocks
text:
4.2 Reaction types

Nucleophiles and electrophiles
Most of the reactions in this book involve the formation of a new covalent bond in which both bonding electrons come from one of the two partners. The partner that supplies the electron pair is the nucleophile, and the partner that accepts it is the electrophile. An electrophile is a reagent that forms a bond to its reaction partner by accepting both bonding electrons from that partner (IUPAC, n.d.f). Nucleophiles are electron-rich: they typically carry a lone pair or a negative charge, as do the oxygen of a hydroxy group, the nitrogen of an amino group, water and the hydroxide ion. Electrophiles are electron-poor: the most important electrophile in this book is the carbon atom of a carbonyl group, which carries a partial positive charge (Section 4.1). The nucleophilicity of a reagent is its reactivity as a nucleophile, measured by comparing the rate constants of its reactions with a common partner (IUPAC, n.d.j).
The rest of this section describes four types of reaction, defined by what happens to the reacting molecules as a whole.


Addition
In an addition reaction, two molecules combine to form a single product, without the loss of any atoms. A characteristic example is the addition of a nucleophile to a carbonyl group. The nucleophile bonds to the carbonyl carbon, one of the two bonds between carbon and oxygen is broken, and the oxygen atom picks up a hydrogen atom to become a hydroxy group (Figure 4.3 a). For example, water adds to formaldehyde to give methanediol, H2C(OH)2, and HCN adds to an aldehyde RCHO to give a cyanohydrin, RCH(OH)CN, a compound in which a hydroxy group and a nitrile group are attached to the same carbon atom. Addition to a carbonyl group creates a new bond to carbon, and therefore lengthens the carbon skeleton when the nucleophile contains carbon. Many of the reactions that build sugars from formaldehyde, described in Section 4.4, are additions of this kind.


Condensation and hydrolysis
A condensation reaction is a reaction in which two or more reactants, or two reactive sites within the same molecule, yield a single main product with the accompanying formation of water or of some other small molecule (IUPAC, n.d.e). The formation of an ester from an acid and an alcohol is a condensation (Figure 4.3 b):
\[
\mathrm{R{-}COOH + HO{-}R' \rightleftharpoons R{-}CO{-}O{-}R' + H_2O} .
\tag{4.1}\]
The reverse reaction, in which a bond is broken by reaction with water, is hydrolysis. Condensation and hydrolysis are central to this book because every link in an RNA chain, and every bond between a nucleobase, ribose and phosphate in a nucleotide, is formed by a condensation and broken by hydrolysis.
Whether a condensation or a hydrolysis is favoured depends on the Gibbs free energy change of the reaction (Section 2.7). For a reaction at equilibrium, the ratio of the activities (effective concentrations) of products to reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation, has a fixed value at a given temperature, called the equilibrium constant, K. For Equation 4.1,
\[
K = \frac{a_\mathrm{ester}\, a_\mathrm{H_2O}}{a_\mathrm{acid}\, a_\mathrm{alcohol}} ,
\tag{4.2}\]
where a denotes activity. The equilibrium constant is related to the standard Gibbs free energy change of the reaction, \(\Delta G^\circ\), by
\[
\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K ,
\tag{4.3}\]
where R is the molar gas constant and T the absolute temperature (Section 2.8). A negative \(\Delta G^\circ\) corresponds to K > 1, which favours products; a positive \(\Delta G^\circ\) to K < 1. At 298.15 K, a reaction with \(\Delta G^\circ\) = +10 kJ mol−1 has K = 0.018, and one with +20 kJ mol−1 has K = 3.1 × 10−4.
Equation 4.2 explains why condensation reactions are difficult in water. In a dilute aqueous solution, water is present in enormous excess: its concentration is about 55 mol per litre (997.05 g L−1 at 25 °C (International Association for the Properties of Water and Steam 2011) divided by its molar mass of 18.015 g mol−1). Every molecule of ester formed must coexist with this large amount of water, which drives the equilibrium of Equation 4.1 back towards hydrolysis. In water, hydrolysis is therefore generally favoured over condensation, even when the condensation itself releases energy in the absence of water. This is one of the central difficulties of prebiotic chemistry, and it explains the interest in settings where water is removed, such as the drying phase of wet-dry cycles (Section 3.7), and in activated reactants that carry a built-in source of free energy (Section 4.6).


Oxidation and reduction
Oxidation and reduction were defined in Section 3.4 as the loss and gain of electrons, followed through oxidation numbers. In organic molecules, oxidation usually means the formation of more bonds from carbon to oxygen (or other electronegative atoms), or fewer bonds from carbon to hydrogen; reduction means the reverse. For example, the oxidation number of carbon increases from −2 in methanol (CH3OH) to 0 in formaldehyde (H2CO) and +2 in formic acid (HCOOH), so the sequence methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid is a series of oxidations. A sugar such as ribose, C5H10O5, has the same ratio of carbon to hydrogen to oxygen as formaldehyde, CH2O, and its average carbon oxidation number is likewise 0.
Redox reactions matter in prebiotic chemistry because the feedstock molecules are not at the same oxidation level as the building blocks. HCN, for example, contains carbon at oxidation number +2, whereas most of the carbon atoms of ribose are at lower oxidation numbers. Converting one into the other requires a reducing agent, such as the hydrogen sulfide used in the reactions of Patel et al. (2015) (Section 3.5).






Figure 4.3: Three reaction types. (a) Addition: a nucleophile (Nu–H) adds to the carbonyl group of an aldehyde, giving a single product in which the carbonyl oxygen has become a hydroxy group. (b) Condensation and hydrolysis: an acid and an alcohol combine to give an ester and water; the reverse reaction is hydrolysis. (c) Oxidation states of carbon in the series methanol, formaldehyde, formic acid.

title: 4  From Simple Molecules to Building Blocks
section: 4.3 The Miller-Urey experiment and its descendants
text:
4.3 The Miller-Urey experiment and its descendants

Amino acids
The first building blocks of life to be made in a laboratory simulation of the early Earth were not components of RNA but amino acids, the units from which proteins are built. An amino acid, in the sense used in biochemistry, is a compound that contains both an amino group and a carboxy group (Section 4.1) attached to the same carbon atom. Its general formula is H2N–CHR–COOH. In the simplest amino acid, glycine, R is a hydrogen atom; in alanine, R is a methyl group, –CH3. Every amino acid except glycine has a stereocentre and therefore exists as two enantiomers (Section 4.1). Although amino acids are not part of RNA, the experiments that produced them established the methods and the questions that later work on RNA has followed, and they are described here for that reason.






TipKey experiment: Miller 1953



In 1953 Stanley Miller, a graduate student working with Harold Urey, published the results of an experiment designed to test whether organic compounds could be formed under conditions then thought to resemble those of the early Earth (Miller 1953). A mixture of methane, ammonia and hydrogen, together with water vapour, was sealed in a glass apparatus (Figure 4.4). Water was boiled in a small flask so that its vapour circulated through a larger flask containing the gases, in which a continuous electric spark was passed between two electrodes to simulate lightning. A condenser cooled the gases, and the water that condensed collected in a U-shaped trap, from which it returned to the boiling flask. Products formed in the gas were thus washed into the liquid, a model of an ocean receiving material from the atmosphere.
After about a week of continuous operation, the solution was analysed by paper chromatography. Using this method, Miller identified glycine, alanine (in two isomeric forms, \(\alpha\)- and \(\beta\)-alanine) and, less certainly, aspartic acid and \(\alpha\)-aminobutyric acid (Miller 1953).
The result showed for the first time that biologically important molecules can be formed from simple gases by a natural energy source, without any biological agency. It transformed the study of the origin of life into an experimental field and established the basis of prebiotic chemistry (Bada 2013).








Figure 4.4: Schematic diagram of the Miller apparatus. Water boiled in the small flask supplies vapour to the large flask, where a spark acts on the gas mixture. The condenser returns water and dissolved products to the trap, from which samples were taken. Arrows show the direction of circulation. The drawing is schematic and not to scale.





How the amino acids form
The spark acts on the gas phase, but the amino acids were collected from the water. Products of the reactions in the gas dissolve in the water and react further in solution. Among the small reactive molecules that can give amino acids in water are aldehydes and hydrogen cyanide (Section 3.6), together with the ammonia of the gas mixture. The route by which these three combine to give an amino acid is the Strecker synthesis, named after Adolph Strecker, who described it in the nineteenth century:

Ammonia adds to the carbonyl group of an aldehyde, RCHO, and water is lost, giving an imine, RCH=NH, a compound with a carbon-nitrogen double bond.
HCN adds to the imine, giving an aminonitrile, RCH(NH2)CN.
Hydrolysis of the nitrile group converts the aminonitrile into the amino acid RCH(NH2)COOH.

With formaldehyde (R = H), the product is glycine; with acetaldehyde (R = CH3), alanine. The sequence uses the reaction types of Section 4.2: addition, condensation and hydrolysis. Because the starting aldehyde is achiral and nothing in the solution favours one enantiomer, the amino acids are formed as racemates.


Later experiments
Miller kept the extracts of many of his experiments. Archived samples, some of which had never been analysed, were found in his laboratory material shortly before his death in May 2007, and have since been analysed with modern methods such as high-performance liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry (Bada 2013; Parker et al. 2011).

One set of experiments from the 1950s used, besides the apparatus of Figure 4.4, one that generated a hot water mist in the spark flask, simulating a volcanic eruption rich in water vapour and accompanied by lightning. Re-analysis of its extracts showed that this “volcanic” apparatus produced a wider variety of amino acids than the classic one (Johnson et al. 2008).
Another, carried out in 1958 but not previously reported, used a gas mixture of hydrogen sulfide (H2S), methane, ammonia and carbon dioxide. Analysis of its residues found 23 amino acids and 4 amines, including 7 compounds containing sulfur; the amino acids with stereocentres were racemic, indicating that they were not contaminants introduced during storage (Parker et al. 2011). The relative abundances of the amino acids were very similar to those in some carbonaceous meteorites (Parker et al. 2011) (Section 3.7).

Taken together, these re-analyses found more than 40 different amino acids and amines, many more than Miller was able to identify with the methods of 1953 (Bada 2013).


What the experiments show
The Miller experiment and its successors show that, given a reducing gas mixture and a source of energy, a variety of organic molecules of biological interest form readily and in the same racemic mixtures that a non-biological origin requires. They also show the limitations of this approach. The yields depend strongly on the composition of the gas: as described in Section 3.4, neutral mixtures of CO2 and N2 give much less, although more than was once thought (Cleaves et al. 2008). And the products are mixtures of many compounds, of which the molecules of interest are only a part. Both points recur in the synthesis of the building blocks of RNA, which is the subject of the remaining sections of this chapter.

title: 4  From Simple Molecules to Building Blocks
section: 4.4 Sugars: the formose reaction and the ribose problem
text:
4.4 Sugars: the formose reaction and the ribose problem

Sugars and ribose
A sugar, or monosaccharide, is a compound of formula Cn(H2O)n, usually with n from 3 to 7, that contains one carbonyl group and a hydroxy group on each of the other carbon atoms. If the carbonyl group is an aldehyde at the end of the chain, the sugar is an aldose; if it is a ketone, the sugar is a ketose. Sugars are named by the number of carbon atoms: trioses (n = 3), tetroses (4), pentoses (5) and hexoses (6). The smallest compound of this type, glycolaldehyde (HOCH2CHO, n = 2), has no stereocentre and is not usually counted as a sugar, but it is the starting point of sugar chemistry under prebiotic conditions.
Ribose, the sugar of RNA, is an aldopentose, C5H10O5. In its open-chain form, three of its carbon atoms (C2, C3 and C4) are stereocentres, so that 23 = 8 stereoisomers share its structural formula: D- and L-ribose, and the D and L forms of three other aldopentoses, arabinose, xylose and lyxose. The D/L label refers to the configuration of the stereocentre furthest from the carbonyl group, compared with that of D-glyceraldehyde (Section 4.1). RNA contains only D-ribose. In D-ribose, all three hydroxy groups on the stereocentres lie on the same side of the chain in the Fischer projection (Figure 4.5 b).
In water, a sugar does not remain in the open-chain form. A hydroxy group of the same molecule adds to the carbonyl group (an addition, Section 4.2), closing a ring. When the hydroxy group on C4 of ribose adds to the aldehyde at C1, the product is a five-membered ring of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, a furanose; addition of the hydroxy group on C5 gives a six-membered ring, a pyranose. The forms interconvert in solution. In RNA, ribose is present as the furanose, with its C1 bonded to a nucleobase and its C5 (and C3) bonded to phosphate (Chapter 5).


The formose reaction
The formose reaction, introduced in Section 3.6, converts formaldehyde into sugars in a basic solution. It is built from one type of carbon-carbon bond-forming step, the aldol reaction: in a basic solution, the carbon atom next to a carbonyl group loses a proton and becomes a nucleophile, which adds to the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule (an electrophile), joining the two carbon skeletons. Formaldehyde, which has no carbon atom next to its carbonyl group, can act only as the electrophile.
The mechanism proposed by Breslow (Breslow 1959) explains why the reaction starts slowly and then accelerates (Figure 4.5 a):

Glycolaldehyde (C2) adds to formaldehyde (aldol reaction), giving glyceraldehyde (C3).
Glyceraldehyde isomerises to dihydroxyacetone (C3), the corresponding ketose.
Dihydroxyacetone adds a second formaldehyde, giving a ketotetrose (C4), which isomerises to an aldotetrose.
The aldotetrose splits in a reverse aldol reaction into two molecules of glycolaldehyde.

Each turn of the cycle consumes two molecules of formaldehyde and converts one molecule of glycolaldehyde into two. The cycle is therefore autocatalytic (Section 2.8): once a little glycolaldehyde is present, its amount grows, and the reaction accelerates. The direct combination of two formaldehyde molecules to give glycolaldehyde is very slow, which is why the reaction has an induction period unless glycolaldehyde is added at the start.
The same aldol and isomerisation steps also join the intermediates to one another and to formaldehyde in many other combinations. The formose reaction therefore yields numerous sugars without any selectivity for ribose (Larralde, Robertson, and Miller 1995), together with branched sugars and, at longer reaction times, compounds that are no longer sugars. Ribose is one product among many.


The stability problem
A second difficulty is that ribose, once formed, does not survive for long.






TipKey experiment: Larralde, Robertson and Miller 1995



Sugars were known to decompose in strong acid or base, but few data existed for neutral solutions. Larralde, Robertson and Miller measured the rate of decomposition of ribose between pH 4 and pH 8 at temperatures from 40 °C to 120 °C (Larralde, Robertson, and Miller 1995). The half-life of ribose at pH 7.0 was 73 minutes at 100 °C, and the value extrapolated to 0 °C was 44 years. The other aldopentoses and aldohexoses, as well as 2-deoxyribose and ribose 5-phosphate, had half-lives within an order of magnitude of these values.
The authors concluded that the backbone of the first genetic material could not have contained ribose or other sugars, because of their instability (Larralde, Robertson, and Miller 1995).


The two half-lives differ by a factor of about 3 × 105. Inserting them into the Arrhenius equation (Section 2.8) gives an apparent activation energy of about 107 kJ mol−1, and, by interpolation, a half-life of the order of one year at 25 °C (Exercise 16). On a geological timescale even the value at 0 °C is short: ribose would have to be used within years to centuries of its formation, or protected.


Proposed solutions
Three types of response to the ribose problem have been proposed.

Stabilisation by minerals. Borate, the anion of boric acid, forms complexes with sugars that have hydroxy groups on adjacent carbon atoms. Ricardo and co-workers reported that borate minerals stabilize ribose (Ricardo et al. 2004). Later experiments by the same group, starting from formaldehyde and glycolaldehyde, showed how borate, molybdate and calcium minerals guide the formation of tetroses, pentoses (including ribose) and heptoses, and suggested that pentoses would have formed as stable borate complexes on the surface of an early Earth (Kim et al. 2011). The stabilisation is not absolute: over longer times, the borate-bound pentoses pass on to other products (Kim et al. 2011). Whether borate minerals were available on the Hadean Earth is itself debated; Kim et al. (2011) argue that they could have formed from hydrated rocks in subduction zones.
Different backbones. The first genetic material may not have contained ribose at all, but a backbone built from a simpler or more stable unit, which was later replaced by ribose-phosphate (Larralde, Robertson, and Miller 1995).
Bypassing free ribose. Ribose need not be formed as a free sugar and then attached to a nucleobase. In the synthesis of Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland (2009), the carbon atoms of the sugar and part of the nucleobase are assembled together, so that free ribose never appears (Chapter 5).

None of these is accepted as a complete solution. The ribose problem illustrates a general difficulty of prebiotic chemistry that recurs in this chapter: reactions that form the right molecule usually form many others as well, and the right molecule is often not stable in the conditions under which it forms.






Figure 4.5: Sugars. (a) The formose cycle proposed by Breslow. Glycolaldehyde (C2) adds formaldehyde (HCHO) to give glyceraldehyde (C3), which isomerises to dihydroxyacetone; a second formaldehyde gives a tetrose (C4), which splits into two glycolaldehyde molecules, so that each turn doubles the glycolaldehyde. (b) D-ribose in the open-chain form (Fischer projection, stereocentres C2 to C4) and as the five-membered furanose ring, the form present in RNA, shown here as the \(\beta\) anomer with the hydrogen atoms on the ring carbons omitted.

title: 4  From Simple Molecules to Building Blocks
text:
4.5 Nucleobases from HCN and formamide

Purines and pyrimidines
The nucleobases of RNA are heterocyclic compounds: their rings contain atoms of at least one element other than carbon, in this case nitrogen. There are two families (Figure 4.6).

Purines have two fused rings, a six-membered ring and a five-membered ring sharing one bond, with nine ring atoms in total, four of them nitrogen. The purines of RNA are adenine (A), C5H5N5, and guanine (G), C5H5N5O.
Pyrimidines have a single six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms, separated by one carbon atom. The pyrimidines of RNA are cytosine (C), C4H5N3O, and uracil (U), C4H4N2O2 (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). In DNA, uracil is replaced by thymine, which carries an additional methyl group.

In RNA, each nucleobase is bonded through one of its ring nitrogen atoms to C1 of ribose (Section 4.4): N9 in the purines and N1 in the pyrimidines. The edges of the bases carry hydrogen-bond donors (N–H) and acceptors (ring N and C=O) (Section 2.5), and it is through these that adenine pairs with uracil and guanine with cytosine, the basis of the copying of genetic information described in later chapters.
The prebiotic problem is different for the two families. The purines can be formed directly from HCN; the pyrimidines require other routes.


Purines from hydrogen cyanide






TipKey experiment: Oró 1960-1961



Around 1960 Joan Oró found that adenine is formed from hydrogen cyanide in concentrated solutions of ammonium cyanide. He published a full account with Kimball in 1961 (Oró and Kimball 1961), together with a proposed mechanism (Oró 1961). The result was surprising because adenine, a molecule central to biology, has the formula C5H5N5, exactly five times that of HCN: it can be regarded as a pentamer of HCN, assembled without the loss of any atom.
Later re-examination of this chemistry found that the yields are low: about 0.1 percent of adenine after hydrolysis of the soluble products, and about 0.05 percent from the insoluble black polymer that also forms (Borquez et al. 2005) (Section 3.6). Guanine is also formed.


The reaction proceeds through intermediates of increasing size. Four HCN molecules combine to give the HCN tetramer, whose structure was established in 1955 as diaminomaleonitrile (DAMN) (Webb, Frank, and Schneider 1955). Further steps, including the incorporation of a fifth HCN unit and the closing of the two rings, lead to adenine; detailed mechanisms have been proposed on the basis of experiments and quantum-chemical calculations (Oró 1961; Roy, Najafian, and Ragué Schleyer 2007).
Because HCN polymerises only when it is concentrated, the reaction requires a mechanism of concentration. One proposal is freezing: when a dilute solution freezes, the dissolved molecules are excluded from the ice and concentrated in the remaining liquid. In the experiment of Levy et al. (2000), introduced in Section 3.7, dilute solutions of ammonium cyanide kept frozen for 25 years gave adenine and guanine in substantial yields.


Pyrimidines
The pyrimidines are not formed in significant amounts from HCN alone. Two routes have been studied, both starting from cyanoacetylene, HC\(\equiv\)C–C\(\equiv\)N, a molecule produced by a spark discharge in a mixture of methane and nitrogen (Robertson and Miller 1995):

Cyanoacetylene reacts with cyanate (NCO−) to give cytosine. This reaction requires cyanate concentrations above 0.1 mol L−1, which are unlikely in water, because cyanate is hydrolysed rapidly to CO2 and NH3 (Robertson and Miller 1995).
Cyanoacetylene is hydrolysed to cyanoacetaldehyde, which reacts with urea, (NH2)2CO. At low concentrations of urea, no detectable cytosine is formed. Robertson and Miller showed that in concentrated urea solution, such as might be found in an evaporating lagoon or in pools on drying beaches, cyanoacetaldehyde gives cytosine in yields of 30 to 50 percent, and uracil is formed from cytosine by hydrolysis (Robertson and Miller 1995).

The second route illustrates again the importance of concentration by evaporation (Section 3.7). The conversion of cytosine into uracil is itself a hydrolysis (Section 4.2): the amino group of cytosine is replaced by a C=O group, with the release of ammonia.


Formamide
Formamide, HCONH2, is the amide of formic acid (Section 4.1) and the product of the addition of water to HCN. It is a liquid between its melting point of 275.7 K (2.6 °C) (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.) and a boiling point of about 484 K (211 °C), calculated from vapour-pressure data (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). Its liquid range thus extends far above that of water, and reactions can be carried out in it at temperatures at which water would boil.
In 2001 Saladino and co-workers reported the synthesis of purine, adenine, cytosine and 4(3H)-pyrimidinone by heating formamide in the presence of simple mineral catalysts (Saladino et al. 2001). Later work examined many other mineral catalysts and energy sources (Saladino et al. 2012), including high-energy chemistry initiated by laser pulses (Ferus et al. 2015). Formamide is attractive as a solvent and reagent because one compound supplies both purines and pyrimidines. Its weakness, as with HCN, is concentration: formamide mixes with water in all proportions, and how a concentrated formamide environment could have arisen on the early Earth is an open question.


Nucleobases from space
Nucleobases have also been found in carbonaceous meteorites. Callahan and co-workers detected a diverse suite of nucleobases in the Murchison meteorite and another meteorite, together with nucleobase analogues that are rare on Earth (Callahan et al. 2011) (Section 3.7). Meteorites may therefore have delivered small amounts of nucleobases to the early Earth, in addition to those formed on its surface.


What remains
Purines can be formed from HCN, and pyrimidines from cyanoacetylene and urea or from formamide. In each case, the bases are formed in mixtures with many other compounds and in low yield unless the reactants are concentrated. More fundamentally, a free nucleobase and a free ribose do not combine efficiently: the addition of nucleobases to ribose is inefficient for the purines and does not occur at all for the pyrimidines of RNA (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009). This problem, and the route that avoids it by building the nucleotide in pieces, are the subject of Chapter 5.






Figure 4.6: The nucleobases of RNA. Purines (top): adenine and guanine, with a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring. Pyrimidines (bottom): cytosine and uracil, with a single six-membered ring. Nitrogen atoms are shown in blue and oxygen atoms in red; the hydrogen atom that is replaced by ribose in RNA (on N9 in purines, N1 in pyrimidines) is marked with an asterisk. Hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon are omitted.

title: 4  From Simple Molecules to Building Blocks
text:
4.6 Phosphate: esters, anhydrides and activation

Phosphoric acid and its esters
The phosphorus of RNA is present as phosphate (Section 3.6). Its parent compound, phosphoric acid, H3PO4, has a phosphorus atom bonded to one oxygen atom by a double bond and to three hydroxy groups. Each of the three hydroxy groups can lose a proton (Section 2.6), so that phosphoric acid is a triprotic acid: depending on the pH, it is present as H3PO4, H2PO4−, HPO42− or PO43−. In neutral water the dominant forms are H2PO4− and HPO42−; the general term phosphate covers all of them.
A hydroxy group of phosphoric acid can condense with the hydroxy group of an alcohol, with the loss of water, to form a phosphate ester (Section 4.2). One such condensation gives a phosphate monoester, R–O–PO32− at neutral pH; a second, with another alcohol, gives a phosphate diester, R–O–PO2−–O–R\('\) (Figure 4.7). In RNA, each phosphate is a diester that joins the C3 hydroxy group of one ribose to the C5 hydroxy group of the next. This linkage, the phosphodiester bond, is the subject of Chapter 6. The addition of a phosphate group to a molecule is called phosphorylation.
Two phosphate groups can also condense with each other. The product, pyrophosphate (diphosphate), contains a P–O–P linkage called a phosphoanhydride bond. Longer chains and rings of phosphate units are called polyphosphates; trimetaphosphate is a ring of three. The hydrolysis of a phosphoanhydride bond releases more free energy than the hydrolysis of a phosphate ester, so that a molecule that contains such a bond can transfer a phosphate group to an alcohol. Phosphoanhydride bonds are the source of free energy in adenosine triphosphate (ATP) in modern cells, and they are an example of the activated reactants introduced in Section 4.2.


Why phosphate?
In an influential essay, Westheimer asked why living organisms use phosphate to link the units of their nucleic acids and to carry many of their metabolites (Westheimer 1987). His answer rested on the charge of phosphate. A phosphate diester, such as the linkage in RNA, still carries one negative charge. The charge keeps the molecule dissolved in water and retained within a cell, and it repels negatively charged nucleophiles such as the hydroxide ion, so that the ester is hydrolysed very slowly. Yet the ester can be made and broken by enzymes when required (Westheimer 1987). No other simple acid combines these properties as well; this is one reason to think that phosphate was part of RNA from the beginning.


Phosphorylation in water
The stability that makes phosphate esters suitable for genetic molecules also makes them difficult to form. The formation of a phosphate ester is a condensation, and like the formation of the ester in Equation 4.1 it is disfavoured in water (Equation 4.2): the equilibrium lies on the side of the free phosphate and the alcohol. In addition, phosphate is scarce and poorly soluble in the presence of calcium (the phosphate problem, Section 3.6). Prebiotic phosphorylation therefore requires either the removal of water or a phosphorus compound that carries its own free energy. Several approaches have been studied.

Heating with urea. Lohrmann and Orgel showed that mixtures of urea and inorganic phosphate can act as prebiotic phosphorylating agents (Lohrmann and Orgel 1971).
Polyphosphates. Volcanic processes can produce polyphosphates, which are activated forms of phosphate (Yamagata et al. 1991).
Reduced phosphorus. The corrosion of schreibersite from meteorites releases reactive phosphorus compounds, including pyrophosphate; schreibersite phosphorylates nucleosides in water (Section 3.6) (Pasek and Lauretta 2005; Gull et al. 2015).
Diamidophosphate. Amidophosphates, in which an amino group replaces a hydroxy group of phosphoric acid, are activated phosphorylating agents (see the key experiment below).







TipKey experiment: Gibard and co-workers 2018



Earlier prebiotic phosphorylation reactions had limited success or required particular environments that are incompatible with the subsequent formation of oligomers (Gibard et al. 2018). Gibard, Bhowmik, Karki, Kim and Krishnamurthy studied diamidophosphate (DAP), PO2(NH2)2−, which can be produced from trimetaphosphate (Gibard et al. 2018). In water, in solution or in a paste, DAP phosphorylated a wide variety of building blocks: nucleosides and nucleotides, amino acids and the precursors of lipids, without the need for an additional condensing agent. Under the same conditions, short chains of nucleotides, short peptides and lipid vesicles were formed (Gibard et al. 2018).
The result showed that a single, plausible phosphorus reagent can phosphorylate the three classes of biological building block in water, and so connect the formation of building blocks with their assembly into larger structures in one environment (Gibard et al. 2018).




What remains
Each approach to phosphorylation solves part of the problem. Dry heating removes water but is hard to combine with the reactions that precede and follow it; polyphosphates, schreibersite and amidophosphates provide activated phosphorus but depend on particular geological sources and settings. Moreover, phosphorylation of a nucleoside can occur at more than one hydroxy group (C2, C3 or C5 of ribose), and RNA requires a specific pattern. This problem of selectivity is the subject of the next section.






Figure 4.7: Phosphorus compounds discussed in this section, drawn in the ionisation states that predominate near neutral pH. (a) Phosphate (HPO42−). (b) A phosphate monoester. (c) A phosphate diester, the linkage between nucleotides in RNA. (d) Pyrophosphate, with a phosphoanhydride (P–O–P) bond. (e) Diamidophosphate (DAP). R and R\('\) denote organic groups.
