title: 4  From Simple Molecules to Building Blocks
text:
4.7 Selectivity, mixtures and homochirality

Mixtures are the default
The preceding sections share a pattern. The spark discharge experiments gave more than 40 amino acids and amines (Bada 2013); the formose reaction yields numerous sugars without selectivity for ribose (Larralde, Robertson, and Miller 1995); the polymerisation of ammonium cyanide gives adenine in yields of about 0.1 percent, the rest being other products (Borquez et al. 2005). This outcome is not a failure of particular experiments but a consequence of the chemistry. Small, reactive molecules such as formaldehyde and HCN can combine in many ways, the number of possible products grows rapidly with their size, and in the absence of a catalyst that favours one route, the products are formed in proportion to their rates of formation and survival. A mixture is the default outcome of prebiotic chemistry.
The building blocks of RNA must nevertheless be assembled from a restricted set of components: one sugar (D-ribose), four nucleobases and phosphate, joined in specific positions. The question of how such a selection could arise is called the problem of selectivity. Three types of answer have been explored.

Selective reactions. Some reactions convert only certain members of a mixture. Springsteen and Joyce showed that ribose can be selectively converted into a derivative and removed from a prebiotic mixture of sugars (Springsteen and Joyce 2004).
Sequences of reactions that pass through the right intermediates. In the synthesis of Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland (2009), the building blocks are assembled in a sequence in which each step uses the product of the previous one; the mixture problem is reduced because the intermediates themselves are formed selectively. The reaction network of Patel et al. (2015), in which precursors of nucleotides, amino acids and lipids all derive from HCN, extends this approach to the three classes of biological building block. These syntheses are described in Chapter 5.
Physical separation. Differences in solubility, volatility, adsorption on minerals or crystallisation can separate compounds formed together. Wet-dry cycles and other physical processes of the settings in Section 3.7 act on mixtures as well as on single compounds.

None of these solves the problem in general. Each requires specific conditions, and each is easier to demonstrate in the laboratory, where the starting materials are pure and their amounts controlled, than in a natural setting where many processes act at once.


Homochirality
A special case of selectivity concerns enantiomers. Syntheses from achiral starting materials give racemates (Section 4.1), yet RNA contains only D-ribose and proteins only L-amino acids. The property of consisting of only one enantiomer is called homochirality. Its origin is an open question, which can be divided into two parts: how a small excess of one enantiomer could arise, and how it could then be amplified.
The composition of a mixture of enantiomers is described by its enantiomeric excess (ee):
\[
\mathrm{ee} = \frac{[\mathrm{L}] - [\mathrm{D}]}{[\mathrm{L}] + [\mathrm{D}]}
\tag{4.4}\]
where [L] and [D] are the concentrations of the two enantiomers. A racemate has ee = 0; a homochiral sample has ee = ±1, often expressed as ±100 percent.
Small initial excesses. Small excesses of one enantiomer may arise from chance fluctuations, which are significant in small numbers of molecules, or from physical influences that distinguish mirror images, such as circularly polarised light. Cronin and Pizzarello reported enantiomeric excesses, favouring the L form, in amino acids of the Murchison meteorite (Cronin and Pizzarello 1997), which suggests that excesses can arise without biology.
Amplification. A small excess becomes significant only if it is amplified. In 1953 Frank proposed a simple reaction scheme in which this occurs spontaneously (Frank 1953). Each enantiomer catalyses its own formation from an achiral reactant (autocatalysis, Section 2.8), and the two enantiomers react with each other to form an inactive product. The enantiomer present in excess then grows at the expense of the other, and the excess is amplified towards homochirality (Figure 4.8). In 1995 Soai and co-workers discovered a real reaction with this property, an asymmetric autocatalysis in which a product with a small enantiomeric excess is formed with a much larger one (Soai et al. 1995).






TipKey experiment: Viedma 2005



Some compounds crystallise as separate crystals of the two mirror-image forms. Viedma studied such a system in which a large population of crystals, initially containing equal numbers of the two forms, was kept in contact with its saturated solution and continuously ground (Viedma 2005). Grinding breaks crystals into fragments that serve as seeds for further growth, while small fragments dissolve and their material is recycled through the solution. Over time, the population moved into complete chiral purity, with one of the two forms disappearing entirely (Viedma 2005).
The experiment showed that total symmetry breaking and complete chiral purity can be achieved from a system that initially contains both forms, through a nonlinear process of autocatalysis and recycling (Viedma 2005). It provided a physical counterpart to Frank’s chemical model.


These mechanisms show that homochirality is not physically improbable once a mechanism of amplification exists. Which mechanism, if any, operated in the origin of RNA is not known. The question is taken up again in Chapter 5, where the chirality of ribose is related to the synthesis of nucleotides.






Figure 4.8: A numerical solution of a Frank-type model of chiral amplification. An achiral reactant A is converted into L or D, each of which catalyses its own formation (rate constant k); L and D react with each other to form an inactive product (rate constant 20k). All amounts are relative to the initial amount of A, and the initial amount of L plus D is 0.01. (a) Amounts of A, L and D for an initial enantiomeric excess of 1 percent. (b) Enantiomeric excess for initial excesses of 1, 0.1 and 0.01 percent; in each case the excess is amplified to 100 percent. The model is illustrative, and its parameters do not represent a specific chemical system.

title: 4  From Simple Molecules to Building Blocks
text:
Summary

Organic molecules can be described as skeletons carrying functional groups, which determine their chemical properties. The functional groups of the building blocks of RNA are hydroxy, carbonyl (aldehyde and ketone), carboxy, amino, amide, nitrile and ester groups, including phosphate esters.
Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Enantiomers are non-superposable mirror images; synthesis from achiral starting materials gives racemates, whereas RNA contains only D-ribose.
Nucleophiles donate an electron pair to electrophiles such as the carbonyl carbon. Addition joins two molecules into one; condensation joins them with the loss of water, and hydrolysis reverses it. In water, hydrolysis is generally favoured, because water is present at about 55 mol per litre.
Oxidation and reduction change the oxidation numbers of carbon; converting feedstock molecules such as HCN into sugars requires reduction.
In 1953 Miller showed that an electric spark acting on a mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour produces amino acids, including glycine and alanine. Re-analyses of his archived samples found more than 40 amino acids and amines, formed as racemates. The Strecker synthesis makes amino acids from aldehydes, ammonia and HCN.
Ribose is an aldopentose with three stereocentres, one of eight stereoisomers. The formose reaction, an autocatalytic cycle of aldol and isomerisation steps, converts formaldehyde into many sugars without selectivity for ribose, and ribose decomposes with a half-life of 73 minutes at 100 °C and pH 7. Proposed responses include stabilisation by borate minerals, alternative backbones and routes that bypass free ribose.
The nucleobases are purines (adenine, guanine) and pyrimidines (cytosine, uracil). Adenine, C5H5N5, is a pentamer of HCN and forms from concentrated ammonium cyanide, in low yield. Cytosine forms from cyanoacetaldehyde in concentrated urea, and uracil from cytosine by hydrolysis. Heated formamide with mineral catalysts gives both purines and pyrimidines. Free nucleobases and ribose do not combine efficiently.
Phosphoric acid forms phosphate monoesters and diesters with alcohols, and phosphoanhydride bonds with itself. The negative charge of the phosphate diester makes RNA soluble and resistant to hydrolysis. Phosphorylation in water is disfavoured; proposed solutions include heating with urea, polyphosphates, schreibersite and diamidophosphate.
Prebiotic reactions give mixtures by default. Selective reactions, reaction sequences that pass through the right intermediates, and physical separation are three responses. Homochirality requires a small initial enantiomeric excess and a mechanism of amplification, such as the autocatalysis of Frank’s model, the Soai reaction or Viedma’s crystal grinding.

title: 4  From Simple Molecules to Building Blocks
text:
Exercises

Identify the functional groups in glycolaldehyde (HOCH2CHO) and in glycine (H2NCH2COOH).
Draw the structures of the two structural isomers of formula C2H6O, and name the family to which each belongs.
Explain why the carbon atom of a carbonyl group carries a partial positive charge.
How many stereocentres does glycolaldehyde have? Does it have enantiomers?
Write the molecular formula of the ester formed from acetic acid (CH3COOH) and methanol (CH3OH), and identify the small molecule released.
Write the equation for the addition of HCN to formaldehyde, and name the functional groups in the product.
A condensation has \(\Delta G^\circ\) = +15 kJ mol−1 at 298.15 K. Calculate its equilibrium constant.
Using Equation 4.2, explain why removing water, for example by evaporation, shifts the equilibrium of an esterification towards the ester.
Assign oxidation numbers to each carbon atom in glycolaldehyde (HOCH2CHO) and in glyceraldehyde (HOCH2CH(OH)CHO).
Identify the nucleophile and the electrophile in the addition of water to formaldehyde.
Write the three steps of the Strecker synthesis of alanine from acetaldehyde (CH3CHO), and classify each step as an addition, a condensation or a hydrolysis.
Explain why the alanine formed in a spark discharge experiment is racemic, and why the racemic composition of the amino acids in Miller’s archived samples argues against contamination.
Which features of Miller’s apparatus (Figure 4.4) correspond to an atmosphere, to lightning and to an ocean? Which processes on the early Earth does the apparatus omit?
Draw the Fischer projections of D-ribose and L-ribose. Which of the stereocentres determines the D/L label?
In the formose cycle (Figure 4.5 a), how many molecules of formaldehyde are consumed for each new molecule of glycolaldehyde? Starting from one molecule of glycolaldehyde, how many are present after 10 turns of the cycle, if every molecule completes each turn and none is lost to side reactions?
Using the half-lives of ribose measured by Larralde and co-workers (73 min at 100 °C and 44 years at 0 °C, pH 7.0), estimate the apparent activation energy of ribose decomposition with the Arrhenius equation, and the half-life at 25 °C. State the assumption on which the estimate rests.
Explain why a reaction that gives ribose as one product among many is a problem for the origin of RNA even if the total yield of sugars is high.
Show that the molecular formulas of adenine and guanine differ by one oxygen atom. Which functional groups distinguish them in Figure 4.6?
Using the molar masses of HCN (27.03 g mol−1) and adenine (135.13 g mol−1), calculate the mass of adenine formed from 1 kg of HCN at a yield of 0.1 percent by mass, and the maximum mass if every HCN molecule were converted into adenine.
Write the equation for the hydrolysis of cytosine (C4H5N3O) to uracil (C4H4N2O2), and identify the other product.
Why does the synthesis of cytosine from cyanoacetaldehyde require a concentrated urea solution? Name two prebiotic settings in which such a solution could form.
Write the equation for the condensation of phosphoric acid with methanol to give methyl phosphate, and identify the bond that is formed.
How many negative charges does the phosphate diester linkage carry at neutral pH? Explain how this charge affects the rate of attack by hydroxide ions.
Using Equation 4.3, calculate the equilibrium constant of a phosphorylation with \(\Delta G^\circ\) = +12 kJ mol−1 at 298.15 K. What does the result imply for phosphorylation in dilute aqueous solution?
Explain why a phosphoanhydride bond can be used to drive the formation of a phosphate ester, whereas inorganic phosphate cannot.
A sample contains 0.52 mol of L-alanine and 0.48 mol of D-alanine. Calculate its enantiomeric excess with Equation 4.4.
In Frank’s model (Figure 4.8), what is the role of the reaction between L and D? What would happen to the enantiomeric excess if this reaction were absent?
Explain why the formose reaction gives many sugars, using the reaction steps of Section 4.4.
Why is selectivity easier to demonstrate in the laboratory than in a natural setting? Give two reasons.

title: 5  Assembling Nucleotides
text:
Learning objectives
After reading this chapter you should be able to:

title: 5  Assembling Nucleotides
text:
Describe the structure of a ribonucleotide, distinguish a nucleoside from a nucleotide, and use the primed numbering of the ribose ring.
Explain why joining a free nucleobase to free ribose is inefficient for purines and fails for the pyrimidines of RNA.
Outline the synthesis of activated pyrimidine ribonucleotides by Powner, Gerland and Sutherland, and the routes to purine nucleosides through formamidopyrimidines.
Explain where and how phosphate is attached to a nucleoside, and why the 2\('\),3\('\)-cyclic phosphate is an activated form.
Explain how the chirality of ribose affects the copying of nucleotide chains, and how wet-dry cycles shift condensation equilibria.

title: 5  Assembling Nucleotides
text:
5.1 Anatomy of a nucleotide

Nucleosides and nucleotides
A nucleoside is a nucleobase (Section 4.5) joined to a sugar. In a ribonucleoside, the sugar is D-ribose in its furanose form (Section 4.4), and the bond joins C1 of the ribose to a ring nitrogen of the base: N9 in the purines and N1 in the pyrimidines. This carbon-nitrogen bond is called the N-glycosidic bond. A nucleotide is a nucleoside that carries one or more phosphate groups (Section 4.6), usually on the hydroxy group at C5 of the ribose. A nucleotide therefore has three parts: a nucleobase, a sugar and a phosphate (Figure 5.1).
To distinguish the atoms of the sugar from those of the base, the carbon atoms of ribose in a nucleoside are numbered with a prime: C1\('\) to C5\('\). The N-glycosidic bond joins C1\('\) to the base; the hydroxy groups of ribose are on C2\('\), C3\('\) and C5\('\); and the ring oxygen links C1\('\) and C4\('\).
The four ribonucleosides of RNA are adenosine, guanosine, cytidine and uridine. The corresponding nucleotides with one phosphate on C5\('\) are the nucleoside 5\('\)-monophosphates, abbreviated AMP, GMP, CMP and UMP. Their formulas follow from the condensation reactions that join their parts (Table 5.1). For example, adenine (C5H5N5) and ribose (C5H10O5) combine with the loss of one molecule of water to give adenosine, C10H13N5O4; adenosine and phosphoric acid (H3PO4) combine with the loss of a second molecule of water to give AMP, C10H14N5O7P.

Configuration at C1\('\)
The formation of the N-glycosidic bond creates a new stereocentre at C1\('\). The base can lie on the same side of the furanose ring as the CH2OH group at C4\('\), or on the opposite side. The two forms are called the \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) anomers, respectively. All the nucleosides of RNA are \(\beta\)-D-ribonucleosides: the base is on the same face of the ring as C5\('\). The \(\alpha\) anomers are diastereomers of the natural nucleosides, not enantiomers, and have different properties. A prebiotic synthesis must therefore control not only which sugar and which base are joined, but also the configuration of the new bond.






Figure 5.1: Anatomy of a ribonucleotide, shown for uridine 5\('\)-monophosphate (UMP). The nucleobase (uracil) is joined through N1 to C1\('\) of \(\beta\)-D-ribofuranose by the N-glycosidic bond; a phosphate group is attached to the oxygen on C5\('\). The base without the phosphate is the nucleoside uridine. Hydrogen atoms on carbon are omitted.

title: 5  Assembling Nucleotides
text:
5.2 The glycosidic bond

A condensation in water
The N-glycosidic bond is formed by a condensation (Section 4.2): the hydroxy group on C1\('\) of ribose and a hydrogen atom on the ring nitrogen of the base are lost as water. Like other condensations, it is disfavoured in water (Equation 4.2), so that the direct reaction of a base with ribose in dilute solution gives little product. The obvious remedy, the removal of water by drying and heating, was explored in early work.
Fuller, Sanchez and Orgel reported a synthesis of purine nucleosides from purines and ribose (Fuller, Sanchez, and Orgel 1972), but this and later attempts showed the reaction to be inefficient. The underlying difficulty was summarised by Powner, Gerland and Sutherland: ribose is difficult to form selectively, and the addition of nucleobases to ribose is inefficient in the case of the purines and does not occur at all in the case of the canonical pyrimidines, cytosine and uracil (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009).


Why the pyrimidines fail
The ring nitrogen of a pyrimidine that must form the glycosidic bond, N1, is a poor nucleophile, because its lone pair is delocalised into the adjacent carbonyl group and the ring. The N1–C1\('\) bond is therefore not formed in detectable amounts (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009), while ribose itself decomposes over the same period (Section 4.4). This combination of a slow desired reaction and faster competing reactions is a recurring form of the selectivity problem of Section 4.7.
The failure of the direct route led to two different strategies. The first constructs the glycosidic bond before the nucleobase is complete, so that the nitrogen that forms the bond is part of a more reactive intermediate. This strategy underlies the pyrimidine synthesis of Section 5.3. The second modifies the base, as in the purine routes through formamidopyrimidines described in the same section.

title: 5  Assembling Nucleotides
text:
5.3 Building the nucleotide in pieces

The strategy
If the complete base and the complete sugar do not combine, the nucleotide can be assembled from smaller pieces, each containing part of the base and part of the sugar. In this approach, the bond that will become the N-glycosidic bond is formed early, between fragments in which the nitrogen atom is still reactive, and the rings of the base and the sugar are completed afterwards. Anastasi and co-workers showed that precursors of nucleosides can be assembled directly from units of two and three carbon atoms (Anastasi et al. 2006), and this work led to the synthesis of activated pyrimidine ribonucleotides described below.






TipKey experiment: Powner, Gerland and Sutherland 2009



Powner, Gerland and Sutherland reported a synthesis of activated pyrimidine ribonucleotides that bypasses both free ribose and the free nucleobases (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009). The starting materials were cyanamide, cyanoacetylene, glycolaldehyde, glyceraldehyde and inorganic phosphate, all regarded as plausible prebiotic feedstock molecules (Section 3.6, Section 4.5).
The sequence passes through two key intermediates (Figure 5.2). Cyanamide and glycolaldehyde give 2-aminooxazole, a small heterocycle that contains the future C1\('\) and C2\('\) of the sugar together with the nitrogen and carbon atoms that will become part of the base. Reaction of 2-aminooxazole with glyceraldehyde, which supplies the remaining three carbon atoms of the sugar, gives a pentose amino-oxazoline; the arabinose isomer, arabinose amino-oxazoline, is carried forward. Cyanoacetylene then adds to complete the pyrimidine ring, giving an anhydronucleoside. Finally, phosphate is attached and the anhydronucleoside is converted into the activated pyrimidine nucleotide (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009).
Phosphate is incorporated only at the last stage, but its presence from the start is essential: it controls three of the earlier reactions by acting as a general acid-base catalyst, a nucleophilic catalyst, a pH buffer and a chemical buffer (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009). The authors concluded that prebiotic syntheses should be studied in mixed chemical systems, in which the reactants for one step can also control others (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009).


The 2009 synthesis changed the questions asked about the origin of RNA. It showed that the failure of the direct coupling of base and sugar need not exclude RNA as the first genetic material, and that the stepwise order in which chemists assemble a molecule need not be the order in which it is formed prebiotically. It also left problems: it produces the pyrimidine nucleotides only, it requires the reactants to be added in a specific order, and its starting materials must be supplied in relatively pure form.






Figure 5.2: Simplified outline of the synthesis of activated pyrimidine ribonucleotides by Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland (2009). Each box names a starting material or an intermediate; the free sugar ribose and the free nucleobases do not appear. Phosphate is present throughout as a catalyst and buffer and is incorporated in the final step.





Routes to the purines
The purines require a different approach. Becker and co-workers described a high-yielding and strictly regioselective route to purine nucleosides (Becker et al. 2016). In this route the purine is not formed first: instead, formamidopyrimidines, pyrimidines that carry the atoms of the future five-membered ring in open form, react with the sugar, and the five-membered ring is closed afterwards. The condensation gives the natural N9 nucleosides selectively (Becker et al. 2016).
The same group later reported a synthesis of the pyrimidine nucleosides from small molecules and ribose, driven solely by wet-dry cycles, and compatible with the purine synthesis, so that all four of the canonical bases could form under one set of conditions (Becker et al. 2019). A key starting material, hydroxylamine or hydroxylamine disulfonate, can form under plausible conditions in the early atmosphere (Becker et al. 2019). In the presence of minerals containing phosphate, the 5\('\)-monophosphates and 5\('\)-diphosphates of the nucleosides also formed selectively in one-pot reactions (Becker et al. 2019).
These two families of route, the cyanamide chemistry of Sutherland and co-workers and the formamidopyrimidine chemistry of Carell and co-workers, differ in their starting materials and conditions. In their published forms, both involve steps in which the experimenter supplies reagents in a controlled order, and how they could proceed together in one natural setting is an open question.

title: 5  Assembling Nucleotides
text:
5.4 Phosphorylation of nucleosides

Three hydroxy groups
A ribonucleoside has three hydroxy groups, at C2\('\), C3\('\) and C5\('\), any of which can be phosphorylated. In RNA, the phosphate diester joins C3\('\) of one nucleotide to C5\('\) of the next (Section 4.6). A prebiotic phosphorylation that attaches phosphate at random would give a mixture of 2\('\)-, 3\('\)- and 5\('\)-monophosphates and of products with more than one phosphate group. The position of phosphorylation is therefore a further question of selectivity (Section 4.7).


The 2\('\),3\('\)-cyclic phosphate
When a phosphate group is attached to C2\('\) or C3\('\), it can condense a second time with the neighbouring hydroxy group, forming a five-membered ring that contains C2\('\), C3\('\), two oxygen atoms and the phosphorus atom. The product is the nucleoside 2\('\),3\('\)-cyclic phosphate (Figure 5.3). The ring is strained, and its opening releases free energy. The cyclic phosphate is therefore an activated form of the nucleotide, able to transfer its phosphate to the 5\('\)-hydroxy group of another nucleotide and so to form a phosphodiester bond without an external source of energy. The activated pyrimidine ribonucleotides of Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland (2009) are cyclic phosphates of this kind.






Figure 5.3: Phosphate groups on a ribonucleoside. The ribose ring of a nucleoside is shown with its three hydroxy-bearing positions. (a) 5\('\)-Monophosphate, the form found in RNA chains. (b) 2\('\),3\('\)-Cyclic phosphate, in which one phosphate bridges C2\('\) and C3\('\) in a five-membered ring; its opening releases free energy and can form a phosphodiester bond. B denotes the nucleobase.





Sources of the phosphate
The approaches to prebiotic phosphorylation introduced in Section 4.6 apply to nucleosides. Schreibersite attaches phosphate groups to adenosine and uridine in water (Gull et al. 2015). Diamidophosphate phosphorylates nucleosides and nucleotides in water or a paste without an additional condensing agent, and under the same conditions forms short chains of nucleotides (Gibard et al. 2018). In the wet-dry cycle chemistry of Becker et al. (2019), phosphate-containing minerals gave 5\('\)-mono- and diphosphates selectively. In each case, the conditions that favour phosphorylation are those that reduce the activity of water: drying, pastes, or the use of an activated phosphorus reagent.

title: 5  Assembling Nucleotides
section: 5.5 Chirality and the copying of nucleotides
text:
5.5 Chirality and the copying of nucleotides

D-ribose in every nucleotide
Each ribonucleotide contains four stereocentres in its sugar, at C1\('\), C2\('\), C3\('\) and C4\('\), and all the nucleotides of an RNA molecule have the same configuration at each of them: they are \(\beta\)-D-nucleotides. The mirror image of a \(\beta\)-D-nucleotide is a \(\beta\)-L-nucleotide. Because syntheses from achiral feedstock molecules give racemates (Section 4.1), a prebiotic nucleotide synthesis that begins with achiral or racemic materials will give equal amounts of D and L nucleotides unless an asymmetric influence acts. In the synthesis of Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland (2009), for example, glyceraldehyde is the only chiral starting material; if it is racemic, so are the products.


Enantiomeric cross-inhibition
The importance of homochirality for RNA appears when nucleotides are joined into chains on a template. A template is an existing chain whose sequence directs the order in which monomers are joined; template-directed copying is the subject of Chapter 8. Joyce and co-workers studied the template-directed formation of chains of guanosine nucleotides on a template of polycytidylic acid, poly(C), using activated monomers of either one or both handedness (Joyce et al. 1984). Their results showed chiral selection: when nucleotides of the opposite handedness were present, they were incorporated at the end of a growing chain and blocked further growth (Joyce et al. 1984). This effect, called enantiomeric cross-inhibition, means that copying is inefficient in a racemic mixture of nucleotides.
Enantiomeric cross-inhibition is both a problem and a possible clue. It shows that a racemic pool of nucleotides is a poor starting point for RNA. But it is also a form of the mutual inhibition between enantiomers in Frank’s model (Section 4.7), and so a possible mechanism of amplification once an excess of one enantiomer exists.

title: 5  Assembling Nucleotides
section: 5.6 Condensation in water and wet-dry cycles
text:
5.6 Condensation in water and wet-dry cycles

Water as a product
Every bond that joins the parts of a nucleotide, and every bond that joins nucleotides into chains, is formed by a condensation that releases water. For a condensation of the form
\[
\mathrm{A{-}OH} + \mathrm{H{-}B} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{A{-}B} + \mathrm{H_2O}
\]
the equilibrium constant can be written in terms of the activity of water, \(a_{\mathrm{w}}\):
\[
K = \frac{[\mathrm{A{-}B}]\, a_{\mathrm{w}}}{[\mathrm{A{-}OH}][\mathrm{H{-}B}]}
\tag{5.1}\]
In dilute solution, \(a_{\mathrm{w}}\) is close to 1, and with K small (Section 4.2) the ratio of product to reactants is small. The activity of water measures its effective concentration relative to pure water; it is reduced when water evaporates and solutes become concentrated, or when the reaction takes place in a film, a paste or the pores of a mineral. At constant K, a tenfold reduction in \(a_{\mathrm{w}}\) increases the equilibrium ratio of product to reactants tenfold. Drying also increases the concentrations of the reactants themselves, which increases the rate of the condensation and, for bimolecular reactions, the fraction of reactants converted.


Wet-dry cycles
A wet-dry cycle alternates between a wet phase, in which reactants are dissolved and transported, and a dry phase, in which condensations are favoured. Such cycles occur naturally at the margins of ponds and in hot-spring settings, where water evaporates and is replenished (Section 3.7) (Damer and Deamer 2020). They combine two requirements that cannot be met at the same time: mobility of the reactants, which requires water, and condensation, which requires its removal. The synthesis of nucleosides by Becker et al. (2019) was driven solely by such cycles.
A simple model shows how cycling accumulates a product. Suppose that, in each dry phase, a fraction f of the remaining reactant is converted into a condensation product, and that in each wet phase a fraction h of the product is hydrolysed back to the reactant. If xn is the fraction of material present as product after n cycles,
\[
x_{n+1} = (1-h)\,[\,x_n + f(1 - x_n)\,]
\tag{5.2}\]
which approaches the steady-state value x* = f(1 − h)/(f + h − fh) after many cycles (Figure 5.4). With f = 0.2 and h = 0.05, for example, x* = 0.19/0.24 \(\approx\) 0.79. The product accumulates to a high fraction even though each dry phase converts only a fifth of the reactant, provided that hydrolysis in the wet phase is slow compared with condensation in the dry phase. If hydrolysis is fast, the steady state is low however many cycles occur. The model is schematic: in real cycles the products also include side products and decomposition products, which accumulate as well.






Figure 5.4: The accumulation of a condensation product in a simple model of wet-dry cycles (Equation 5.2). In each cycle a fraction f = 0.2 of the remaining reactant is converted in the dry phase, and a fraction h of the product is hydrolysed in the wet phase. Curves are shown for h = 0.02, 0.05 and 0.2; dashed lines mark the steady states.

title: 5  Assembling Nucleotides
text:
Summary

A nucleoside is a nucleobase joined by an N-glycosidic bond from N9 (purines) or N1 (pyrimidines) to C1\('\) of \(\beta\)-D-ribofuranose; a nucleotide carries in addition one or more phosphate groups, usually on C5\('\).
The direct condensation of a free base with free ribose is inefficient for the purines and does not occur for the canonical pyrimidines.
Powner, Gerland and Sutherland (2009) made activated pyrimidine ribonucleotides from cyanamide, cyanoacetylene, glycolaldehyde, glyceraldehyde and phosphate, through 2-aminooxazole, arabinose amino-oxazoline and an anhydronucleoside, bypassing free ribose and free bases. Carell and co-workers developed routes to purine nucleosides through formamidopyrimidines and a wet-dry cycle synthesis compatible with all four bases.
Phosphorylation can occur at C2\('\), C3\('\) or C5\('\); the 2\('\),3\('\)-cyclic phosphate is an activated form of the nucleotide.
Nucleotides of the wrong handedness block template-directed chain growth (enantiomeric cross-inhibition), so copying requires homochiral nucleotides.
Condensations are favoured when the activity of water is low. Wet-dry cycles combine mobility in the wet phase with condensation in the dry phase, and can accumulate products when hydrolysis is slow.

title: 5  Assembling Nucleotides
text:
Exercises

Write the equation for the condensation of cytosine with ribose to give cytidine, and verify the formula of cytidine in Table 5.1.
Calculate the molar mass of guanosine 5\('\)-monophosphate from the abridged standard atomic weights, and compare it with Table 5.1.
How many stereocentres does the ribose of a nucleoside contain? How many stereoisomers of adenosine are possible in principle?
Explain the difference between the \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) anomers of a nucleoside. Are they enantiomers?
In the synthesis of Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland (2009), which starting materials supply the atoms of the sugar, and which supply the atoms of the base?
Phosphate is incorporated into the nucleotide only in the final step of the 2009 synthesis. Explain why its presence from the start was nevertheless essential.
Draw the 2\('\)-, 3\('\)- and 5\('\)-monophosphates of uridine, and the 2\('\),3\('\)-cyclic phosphate. Which of them is activated, and why?
Explain, with reference to Equation 5.1, why a paste or a film of reactants favours phosphorylation more than a dilute solution.
Explain how enantiomeric cross-inhibition could both hinder and help the origin of homochiral RNA.
Using Equation 5.2, derive the expression for the steady-state fraction x* by setting xn+1 = xn.
For f = 0.2, calculate x* for h = 0.02 and h = 0.2. How many cycles are needed in each case for x to reach 90 percent of x*, starting from x0 = 0?
Name two simplifications of the model of Equation 5.2, and explain how each would change the predicted accumulation of product.

title: 6  Joining Nucleotides into Chains
text:
Learning objectives
After reading this chapter you should be able to:

title: 6  Joining Nucleotides into Chains
text:
Describe the phosphodiester bond and the 5\('\) to 3\('\) direction of an RNA chain, and write sequences in the standard notation.
Explain why the polymerisation of nucleotides in water requires activated monomers, and describe phosphorimidazolides and cyclic phosphates.
Describe the competition between chain growth and hydrolysis, and explain why it limits chain length in dilute solution.
Describe how mineral surfaces, ice and wet-dry cycles favour polymerisation, with reference to key experiments.
Calculate chain length distributions from a probability of extension, and explain why long chains are rare.

title: 6  Joining Nucleotides into Chains
text:
6.1 The phosphodiester bond

Structure of an RNA chain
An RNA molecule is a chain of nucleotides (Section 5.1) joined by phosphodiester bonds. Each phosphate group is esterified twice (Section 4.6): once to the 3\('\)-hydroxy group of one nucleotide and once to the 5\('\)-hydroxy group of the next. The alternating sugar and phosphate units form the backbone of the chain, and the nucleobases are attached to it as side groups at C1\('\) of each ribose (Figure 6.1). Each phosphodiester carries one negative charge at neutral pH (Section 4.6).
Because the two ends of each nucleotide unit differ, the chain has a direction. One end carries a free 5\('\) group (often a phosphate), and the other a free 3\('\)-hydroxy group. By convention, sequences are written from the 5\('\) end to the 3\('\) end, using the one-letter abbreviations of the nucleobases: 5\('\)-AGCU-3\('\) denotes a chain of four nucleotides in which adenosine carries the free 5\('\) end and uridine the free 3\('\) end. A short chain is called an oligonucleotide, often with the number of units given, as in a 10-mer; a long one a polynucleotide.


3\('\),5\('\) and 2\('\),5\('\) linkages
Ribose has hydroxy groups on both C2\('\) and C3\('\), and a phosphodiester can be formed with either. Natural RNA contains only 3\('\),5\('\) linkages. A non-enzymatic polymerisation, in contrast, can form 2\('\),5\('\) linkages as well, and the proportion of each depends on the conditions and on the activating group. Ferris reviewed evidence that montmorillonite-catalysed oligomerisation shows selectivity in the linkages formed, as well as in sequence and in the handedness of the monomers incorporated (Ferris 2006). The regiochemistry of the linkage is therefore another dimension of the selectivity problem (Section 4.7).
The 2\('\)-hydroxy group also makes RNA more labile than DNA, which lacks it. In basic solution, the 2\('\)-oxygen can attack the neighbouring phosphorus atom, breaking the chain by transesterification and leaving a 2\('\),3\('\)-cyclic phosphate at the end of one fragment (Section 5.4) (Li and Breaker 1999). RNA is therefore both formed and broken through the same cyclic intermediate.






Figure 6.1: A dinucleotide, 5\('\)-ApU-3\('\), shown schematically. The phosphodiester bond joins O3\('\) of adenosine to O5\('\) of uridine; the backbone runs from the free 5\('\) end (left) to the free 3\('\) end (right). The 2\('\)-hydroxy groups, which distinguish RNA from DNA, are shown on each ribose. B denotes a nucleobase.

title: 6  Joining Nucleotides into Chains
text:
6.2 Activated nucleotides

Why activation is needed
The formation of a phosphodiester bond from a nucleoside monophosphate and the hydroxy group of another nucleotide is a condensation, and in water its equilibrium lies on the side of the separated monomers (Section 4.2, Section 5.6). In living cells the energy is supplied by nucleoside triphosphates, whose phosphoanhydride bonds are broken as each nucleotide is added. In prebiotic chemistry, the monomers must be activated: the phosphate must carry a group that is easily displaced, a leaving group, so that the attack of a hydroxy group on phosphorus is favourable.


Phosphorimidazolides
The most widely used activated monomers in laboratory studies are nucleoside 5\('\)-phosphorimidazolides, in which one oxygen of the 5\('\)-phosphate is replaced by a nitrogen atom of imidazole or a substituted imidazole such as 2-methylimidazole. Imidazole is a five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms. Imidazole is a good leaving group, so that the 3\('\)-hydroxy group of a neighbouring nucleotide can attack the phosphorus and displace it, forming a phosphodiester bond.
Activated monomers of this kind made possible the study of template-directed synthesis, the copying of a sequence without enzymes. Inoue and Orgel showed that templates containing mainly cytidine direct the synthesis of oligonucleotides from mixtures of activated mononucleotides (Inoue and Orgel 1983). A nucleotide was incorporated into the products if and only if its complement was present in the template, the reaction had high fidelity, and the products had mean chain lengths of six to ten nucleotides (Inoue and Orgel 1983). This chemistry is the subject of Section 8.2.


Cyclic phosphates
The 2\('\),3\('\)-cyclic phosphates of Section 5.4 are a second type of activated nucleotide. They are formed directly in some prebiotic nucleotide syntheses (Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland 2009), and their ring strain supplies the energy for phosphodiester formation.
The problem with all activated monomers is that the same reactivity that allows them to form phosphodiester bonds also allows water to attack them. Every activated monomer can either join a chain or be hydrolysed back to an inactive nucleoside monophosphate.

title: 6  Joining Nucleotides into Chains
text:
6.3 Polymerisation versus hydrolysis

A kinetic competition
Consider an activated monomer M* in solution together with growing chains. In a short time interval, a given M* can react with the end of a chain (rate constant kp, proportional to the concentration of chain ends) or with water (rate constant kh). The probability that it joins a chain rather than being hydrolysed is
\[
p = \frac{k_{\mathrm{p}}\,[\mathrm{ends}]}{k_{\mathrm{p}}\,[\mathrm{ends}] + k_{\mathrm{h}}}
\tag{6.1}\]
where [ends] is the concentration of chain ends that can accept a monomer. Water is present at about 55 mol L−1 (Section 4.2), whereas the concentration of chain ends in a dilute prebiotic solution is small. Even if a chain end is much more reactive than a water molecule, hydrolysis can dominate.
The experimental consequence was stated by Monnard, Kanavarioti and Deamer: in simulations of polymerisation, dilute solutions of activated mononucleotides in the millimolar range hydrolyse extensively, and only trace amounts of dimers and trimers are formed (Monnard, Kanavarioti, and Deamer 2003). Similarly, Ferris and co-workers found that reactions in solution produce only short oligomers, the longest typically being a 10-mer (Ferris et al. 1996).


Ways to win the competition
Equation 6.1 shows two ways to increase p: increase the concentration of chain ends and monomers, or decrease the rate of hydrolysis. The settings discussed in the remainder of this chapter do one or both:

Mineral surfaces adsorb monomers and chains, concentrating them in a thin layer and holding them in favourable orientations (Section 6.4).
Ice excludes solutes as it freezes, concentrating them in liquid channels between ice crystals, and the low temperature slows hydrolysis (Section 6.5).
Drying removes water, reducing its activity and concentrating the reactants (Section 6.6).

title: 6  Joining Nucleotides into Chains
text:
6.4 Help from surfaces: montmorillonite
Clay minerals are layered silicates formed by the weathering of rocks in water. Montmorillonite is a clay mineral whose layers of aluminium silicate carry a negative charge, balanced by cations held between the layers. Organic molecules, including nucleotides, can enter the spaces between the layers and adsorb on their surfaces. Montmorillonite forms by the alteration of volcanic ash, and clays are expected to have been common on the early Earth wherever rocks were weathered by water.






TipKey experiment: Ferris, Hill, Liu and Orgel 1996



Most theories of the origin of biological organisation assume that polymers of 30 to 60 monomers are needed to make a genetic system viable, but such polymers had not been formed by condensation in aqueous solution, because hydrolysis competes with polymerisation (Ferris et al. 1996). Ferris and co-workers studied the oligomerisation of activated monomers, both nucleotides and amino acids, in the presence of minerals: montmorillonite for the nucleotides, and illite and hydroxylapatite for the amino acids (Ferris et al. 1996).
In solution, the reactions produced only short oligomers, the longest typically a 10-mer. In the presence of the mineral surfaces, oligomers up to 55 monomers long were formed. The long chains were obtained by successive “feedings” with fresh monomers: the mineral with its adsorbed chains was repeatedly supplied with activated monomer, and polymerisation took place on the surface in a manner akin to the solid-phase synthesis of biopolymers (Ferris et al. 1996).


The experiment showed that chains in the length range thought necessary for a genetic system can be formed without enzymes. It also showed the price: the monomers were activated, and they were supplied repeatedly. The repeated feeding is a laboratory counterpart of a natural setting in which fresh activated monomers arrive continuously, for example from the processes of Chapter 5, while the growing chains remain bound to a mineral.

title: 6  Joining Nucleotides into Chains
text:
6.5 Help from ice: eutectic concentration
When a dilute aqueous solution is cooled below its freezing point, pure ice crystallises first. The solutes are excluded from the ice and accumulate in the remaining liquid, whose freezing point falls as its concentration rises. At a sufficiently low temperature, the system consists of ice crystals and a network of concentrated liquid channels between them, the eutectic phase. The concentration of solutes in these channels can exceed that of the original solution by orders of magnitude (Section 3.7).






TipKey experiment: Monnard, Kanavarioti and Deamer 2003



Monnard, Kanavarioti and Deamer froze dilute solutions of activated mononucleotides together with the metal-ion catalysts Mg(II) and Pb(II), and kept them at −18 °C for periods up to 38 days (Monnard, Kanavarioti, and Deamer 2003). Under these conditions the monomers were concentrated in eutectic phases within the ice matrix. The hydrolysis of the activated monomers was suppressed at the low temperatures, and polymerisation was enhanced, with yields up to 90 percent (Monnard, Kanavarioti, and Deamer 2003).
The products were random RNA analogues with mixed sequences, 5- to 17-mers with traces of longer products, and purine and pyrimidine bases were incorporated at comparable rates and yields (Monnard, Kanavarioti, and Deamer 2003). The authors suggested that ice deposits on the early Earth could have facilitated the synthesis of short and medium-sized random-sequence RNA analogues (Monnard, Kanavarioti, and Deamer 2003).


Ice thus addresses both terms of Equation 6.1: it concentrates the reactants, increasing kp[ends], and lowers the temperature, decreasing kh (Section 2.8). The equal incorporation of purines and pyrimidines is also significant, since a polymerisation that strongly favoured one type of base would produce chains with little diversity of sequence.

title: 6  Joining Nucleotides into Chains
text:
6.6 Help from cycles
The wet-dry cycles of Section 5.6 apply to polymerisation as well as to the formation of nucleotides. In the dry phase, the activity of water is low and condensation is favoured; in the wet phase, monomers and chains are redistributed and new material is supplied. Freeze-thaw cycles combine the eutectic concentration of Section 6.5 with periodic mixing, and temperature cycles can separate the strands of double-stranded products, a step needed for copying (Section 8.3). Repeated cycles can accumulate longer chains only if the bonds formed in the favourable phase survive the unfavourable one; in the model of Equation 5.2, this requires the hydrolysis fraction h to be small compared with the conversion fraction f.
Cycles also introduce a form of selection. Chains that are more resistant to hydrolysis, because of their sequence, their folding or their binding to a surface, survive more cycles and so accumulate. This link between chemical stability and persistence is a first step from chemistry towards the selection of sequences discussed in Chapters 7 and 8.

title: 6  Joining Nucleotides into Chains
text:
6.7 Chain length distributions

The geometric distribution
Suppose that each time a chain end is offered a monomer, it is extended with probability p and terminated (by hydrolysis of the activated monomer, by blocking of the end, or by any other process) with probability 1 − p, independently of its length. A chain that has reached length n is then extended to n + 1 with probability p. The fraction of chains that reach at least length n is pn−1, and the fraction that have exactly length n is
\[
P(n) = (1-p)\,p^{\,n-1}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots
\tag{6.2}\]
This is the geometric distribution. Its mean is
\[
\langle n \rangle = \frac{1}{1-p}
\tag{6.3}\]
so that p = 0.5 gives a mean length of 2, p = 0.9 a mean of 10, and p = 0.95 a mean of 20 (Figure 6.2).


Why long chains are rare
Equation 6.2 decreases exponentially with n. With p = 0.9, the fraction of chains that reach a length of at least 30 is 0.929 \(\approx\) 0.047, and the fraction that reach 55 is 0.954 \(\approx\) 0.0034. With p = 0.5, as in a dilute solution where hydrolysis competes on equal terms, the fraction that reach 30 is 0.529 \(\approx\) 1.9 × 10−9. Long chains require p close to 1, and a small change in p near 1 has a large effect on the abundance of long chains. This is why the methods of the preceding sections, which raise p, are decisive, and why repeated feeding, as in the experiment of Ferris et al. (1996), can extend chains far beyond the length reached in a single exposure to monomer.
The simple model omits several effects: the rate of extension may depend on chain length and sequence; chains may be broken by hydrolysis of the backbone as well as terminated; and chains may join end to end. More detailed models treat each reaction as a random event occurring at a rate, and follow the populations of chains of each length by stochastic simulation. The qualitative conclusion is the same: without a mechanism that strongly favours extension, the products are dominated by short chains.






Figure 6.2: Chain length distributions predicted by the geometric model (Equation 6.2). (a) Fraction of chains of exactly length n, for probabilities of extension p = 0.5, 0.8, 0.9 and 0.95. (b) Fraction of chains that reach at least length n, on a logarithmic scale; dotted lines mark lengths 30 and 55.

title: 6  Joining Nucleotides into Chains
text:
Summary

In RNA, phosphodiester bonds join the 3\('\)-hydroxy group of one nucleotide to the 5\('\)-hydroxy group of the next; chains have a 5\('\) to 3\('\) direction. Non-enzymatic polymerisation can also form 2\('\),5\('\) linkages, and the 2\('\)-hydroxy group makes RNA susceptible to cleavage.
Polymerisation in water requires activated monomers, such as nucleoside 5\('\)-phosphorimidazolides or 2\('\),3\('\)-cyclic phosphates. Templates direct the incorporation of complementary nucleotides with high fidelity.
Activated monomers are also hydrolysed. In dilute millimolar solutions hydrolysis dominates, and only short oligomers form.
Montmorillonite with repeated feeding of activated monomers gives oligomers up to 55 units long; ice eutectic phases at −18 °C give 5- to 17-mers in yields up to 90 percent; wet-dry and freeze-thaw cycles combine concentration with mixing.
If each extension succeeds with probability p, chain lengths follow a geometric distribution with mean 1/(1 − p); long chains require p close to 1.

title: 6  Joining Nucleotides into Chains
text:
Exercises

Write the sequence of the chain complementary to 5\('\)-AGGCU-3\('\), using the base pairs A–U and G–C, in the 5\('\) to 3\('\) direction.
How many phosphodiester bonds does a linear 20-mer contain? How many negative charges does its backbone carry at neutral pH if both ends carry free hydroxy groups?
Explain why RNA is more easily cleaved in basic solution than DNA.
In a phosphorimidazolide, which bond is broken when a phosphodiester bond forms? What is the leaving group?
Using Equation 6.1, calculate p when kp[ends] = kh, and when kp[ends] = 9kh. What mean chain lengths do these values give according to Equation 6.3?
Explain why freezing a dilute solution can both concentrate the reactants and slow hydrolysis.
In the experiment of Ferris et al. (1996), why were successive “feedings” with monomers needed to obtain chains of 55 units?
Using Equation 6.2, calculate the fraction of chains of length at least 10 for p = 0.8 and for p = 0.95.
Show that the mean of the geometric distribution is 1/(1 − p). (Hint: use \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n x^{n-1} = 1/(1-x)^2\) for \(|x| < 1\).)
Name two effects omitted from the geometric model, and state for each whether including it would increase or decrease the abundance of long chains.

title: 7  Folding into Shapes
text:
Learning objectives
After reading this chapter you should be able to:

title: 7  Folding into Shapes
text:
Describe the Watson-Crick base pairs and the G·U wobble pair, and explain why paired strands are antiparallel.
Explain how base stacking and base pairing together stabilise a double helix, and calculate the free energy of a short helix with the nearest-neighbour model.
Relate the free energy of a structure to the fraction of molecules that adopt it, and define the melting temperature.
Name and recognise the elements of RNA secondary structure, and write a structure in dot-bracket notation.
Explain the principle of minimum free energy structure prediction.
Define a ribozyme, describe the discovery of catalytic RNA, and explain how in vitro selection isolates functional molecules from random sequences.
Estimate the size of sequence space, and discuss what is known about how common folded and functional sequences are within it.

title: 7  Folding into Shapes
text:
7.1 Base pairing

Complementary bases
A single RNA chain (Section 6.1) is flexible. What gives it a defined shape is the ability of its nucleobases (Section 4.5) to form specific hydrogen-bonded pairs (Section 2.5). Two nucleobases joined in this way form a base pair.
The pairs found in double helices of nucleic acids were proposed by Watson and Crick in their model of DNA (Watson and Crick 1953): adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine with cytosine. In RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine. The Watson-Crick base pairs of RNA are therefore A–U, held by two hydrogen bonds, and G–C, held by three (Figure 7.1 a). In each pair a purine faces a pyrimidine, so that both pairs have nearly the same width, and a helix built from any sequence of them has a regular shape. Two sequences that can form Watson-Crick pairs along their whole length are called complementary.
RNA also forms a third pair, between guanine and uracil, held by two hydrogen bonds. In this pair the two bases are shifted relative to each other compared with a Watson-Crick pair; it is called the G·U wobble pair (Figure 7.1 a). G·U pairs occur frequently within RNA helices and are included in the energy parameters used below (Turner and Mathews 2010). In the notation of this book, a dash (A–U) marks a Watson-Crick pair and a centred dot (G·U) a wobble pair.






Figure 7.1: (a) The three base pairs of RNA helices and the number of hydrogen bonds in each: the Watson-Crick pairs A–U and G–C, and the G·U wobble pair. (b) A duplex of 5\('\)-GGACUC-3\('\) with its complementary strand. The two strands run in opposite directions.





Antiparallel strands
Base pairs form only when the two strands are antiparallel: one runs from 5\('\) to 3\('\) in one direction, the other from 5\('\) to 3\('\) in the opposite direction (Figure 7.1 b). Thus 5\('\)-GGACUC-3\('\) pairs with 5\('\)-GAGUCC-3\('\), which is its complement read in the 5\('\) to 3\('\) direction. When a single chain folds back on itself, its two paired segments are antiparallel for the same reason. The paired region winds into a right-handed double helix. A molecule made of two separate strands held together by base pairs is called a duplex.

title: 7  Folding into Shapes
text:
7.2 Duplex stability

Stacking and pairing
Hydrogen bonds alone do not explain why a double helix is stable. When a helix forms, the hydrogen bonds that each base made with water before pairing are replaced by hydrogen bonds to its partner, so the net gain in hydrogen bonding is small. A large part of the stability of a helix comes from base stacking: the flat aromatic rings of neighbouring base pairs lie on top of each other, face to face, along the axis of the helix. Stacking is favoured by dispersion forces between the rings and by the hydrophobic effect (Section 2.5), which drives the non-polar faces of the bases out of contact with water. The contribution of a base pair therefore depends on its neighbours, not only on its own identity.


The nearest-neighbour model
The nearest-neighbour model expresses this dependence quantitatively. The standard Gibbs energy change (Section 2.7) for forming a helix is written as a sum of terms, one for each pair of adjacent base pairs, called a stack, plus a term for starting the helix:
\[
\Delta G^\circ_{\text{helix}} = \Delta G^\circ_{\text{init}} + \sum_{\text{stacks}} \Delta G^\circ_{\text{stack}}
\tag{7.1}\]
The stack terms have been measured by optical melting experiments on many short duplexes and are collected in the Nearest Neighbor Database (Turner and Mathews 2010). The current set of RNA parameters is the 2004 set of Turner and co-workers (Mathews et al. 2004). Table 7.1 lists the values for the ten distinct Watson-Crick stacks at 37 °C. The parameters are given in the literature in kcal mol−1; they are converted here to kJ mol−1 (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ).



Table 7.1: Free energies of the ten Watson-Crick stacks of RNA at 37 °C, Turner 2004 parameters (Mathews et al. 2004; Turner and Mathews 2010), as distributed with the ViennaRNA package (Lorenz et al. 2011). Each stack is written as the top strand 5\('\) to 3\('\) over the bottom strand 3\('\) to 5\('\); a stack read from the other strand is identical (for example 5\('\)-GG-3\('\)/3\('\)-CC-5\('\) is the same as 5\('\)-CC-3\('\)/3\('\)-GG-5\('\)).

Three features of the table are important for what follows. All stacks have negative ΔG°, so every additional base pair stabilises a helix. Stacks containing two G–C pairs are the most stable, and stacks of two A–U pairs the least; the difference is up to a factor of about four. And the order of the bases matters: 5\('\)-GC-3\('\)/3\('\)-CG-5\('\) (−14.2 kJ mol−1) is more stable than 5\('\)-CG-3\('\)/3\('\)-GC-5\('\) (−10.0 kJ mol−1), although both contain the same two pairs.
For two separate strands, the initiation term is positive. It reflects the cost of bringing two independent molecules together into one complex. In the Turner 2004 set it is +4.09 kcal mol−1 (+17.1 kJ mol−1) (Turner and Mathews 2010). As an example, the duplex of Figure 7.1 b contains five stacks, whose values from Table 7.1 sum to −12.4 kcal mol−1 (−51.9 kJ mol−1). With the initiation term, Equation 7.1 gives ΔG°37 \(\approx\) −8.3 kcal mol−1, or −34.8 kJ mol−1. The same value is obtained with the duplex routine of ViennaRNA.


From free energy to populations
A free energy determines what fraction of molecules adopt a structure. For a molecule that is either folded (F) or unfolded (U), with ΔG = GF − GU, the ratio of the two populations at equilibrium is [F]/[U] = exp(−ΔG/RT), where R is the molar gas constant and T the absolute temperature (Section 2.8). The fraction folded, \(\theta\), is therefore
\[
\theta = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(\Delta G / RT)}
\tag{7.2}\]
At 37 °C, RT = 8.314 × 310.15 J mol−1 = 2.58 kJ mol−1. A structure that is 10 kJ mol−1 more stable than the unfolded state is present in about 98 percent of molecules; one that is 20 kJ mol−1 more stable, in more than 99.9 percent.


Melting temperature
ΔG depends on temperature through ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (Section 2.7). Forming a helix releases enthalpy (ΔH < 0, from stacking and pairing) and lowers the entropy (ΔS < 0, because the chain becomes ordered). At low temperature the enthalpy term dominates and the helix is stable; at high temperature the entropy term dominates and it falls apart. The temperature at which ΔG = 0, so that half of the molecules are folded in the two-state model, is the melting temperature, Tm = ΔH/ΔS.
Figure 7.2 shows this behaviour for the 12-nucleotide chain 5\('\)-GGACUUCGGUCC-3\('\), which folds back on itself into a stem of four base pairs closed by the four-nucleotide loop UUCG. The stem contributes three stacks (−13.8, −10.0 and −9.2 kJ mol−1 from Table 7.1, total −33.1 kJ mol−1) and the loop a destabilising +15.5 kJ mol−1, giving ΔG°37 = −17.6 kJ mol−1. Because the two halves belong to one molecule, there is no intermolecular initiation term. From the computed values at 25 °C (−25.4 kJ mol−1) and 60 °C (−2.6 kJ mol−1), the line of Figure 7.2 a gives ΔS \(\approx\) −0.65 kJ K−1 mol−1 and ΔH \(\approx\) −220 kJ mol−1, so that Tm = ΔH/ΔS \(\approx\) 337 K, or 64 °C. The full calculation, which also includes partly paired alternative structures, gives the melting curve of Figure 7.2 b, in which half of the molecules are completely unpaired at 65 °C.






Figure 7.2: Melting of the hairpin 5\('\)-GGACUUCGGUCC-3\('\), calculated with the ViennaRNA package 2.7.2 (Lorenz et al. 2011) and the Turner 2004 parameters (Mathews et al. 2004). (a) Gibbs energy of the hairpin structure relative to the unfolded chain. (b) Fraction of molecules with at least one base pair, from the partition function (Section 7.4); the dotted line marks one half.



Two consequences matter for the origin of life. First, short helices are only marginally stable: a stem of four base pairs melts at about 64 °C, and one of two or three base pairs does not form at all at ordinary temperatures. Second, the melting temperature rises with the length and G–C content of a helix. A hot environment therefore favours single strands, and a cool one favours folded structures and duplexes; this trade-off returns in Section 8.3, where two strands must be separated in order to be copied.

title: 7  Folding into Shapes
text:
7.3 Secondary structure

Definitions
The set of base pairs formed by an RNA molecule is its secondary structure. The three-dimensional arrangement of its atoms is its tertiary structure. The secondary structure is usually restricted to pairs that are nested: if nucleotide i pairs with j, and k pairs with l, with i < k, then either i < k < l < j (one pair lies inside the other) or i < j < k < l (the pairs lie side by side). Pairs that cross, with i < k < j < l, form a pseudoknot; pseudoknots occur in natural RNAs but are excluded from the standard prediction methods described below. A hairpin loop must contain at least three unpaired nucleotides, because a shorter loop cannot span the distance between the two strands of a helix (Turner and Mathews 2010).
A nested secondary structure can be written in dot-bracket notation: a string of the same length as the sequence, in which each paired nucleotide is shown by a bracket, opening for the 5\('\) partner and closing for the 3\('\) partner, and each unpaired nucleotide by a dot. The hairpin of Figure 7.2 is written
GGACUUCGGUCC
((((....))))


Structural elements
A nested secondary structure can be decomposed uniquely into a small set of elements (Figure 7.3):

A helix, or stem, is a run of consecutive stacked base pairs.
A hairpin loop is a loop of unpaired nucleotides closed by a single base pair at the end of a helix.
A bulge is a loop between two helices with unpaired nucleotides on one strand only.
An internal loop is a loop between two helices with unpaired nucleotides on both strands.
A multibranch loop, or junction, is a loop from which three or more helices radiate.
The exterior loop contains the unpaired nucleotides that are not enclosed by any base pair, including the two ends of the chain.

In the energy model, every stack contributes the negative free energy of Table 7.1, and every loop contributes a positive free energy, which accounts for the entropy lost when the unpaired nucleotides are held in a closed ring. The loop terms depend on the size and type of the loop and, for some small loops, on their sequence (Turner and Mathews 2010). The stability of a structure is the sum of all these terms.






Figure 7.3: Elements of RNA secondary structure in a 74-nucleotide example structure, drawn with the coordinate layout of the ViennaRNA package (Lorenz et al. 2011). Paired nucleotides are connected by short lines across each helix.

title: 7  Folding into Shapes
text:
7.4 Predicting structure

The number of possible structures
How many secondary structures can a chain form? If any two nucleotides could pair, subject only to nesting and the minimum hairpin loop of three, a simple recursion gives 65 possible structures for a chain of 10 nucleotides, about 1.1 × 105 for 20, 6.3 × 1011 for 40 and 5.6 × 1025 for 80 (author’s calculation). The number grows roughly by a constant factor with each added nucleotide, that is, exponentially. Base-pairing rules exclude most of these structures for a given sequence, but far too many remain to be examined one by one.


Minimum free energy folding
Under the conditions of a folding experiment, a molecule is expected to spend most of its time in the structure of lowest Gibbs energy, the minimum free energy (MFE) structure, if that structure is clearly more stable than all others (Equation 7.2). Zuker and Stiegler showed in 1981 that the MFE structure can be found without listing all structures, by dynamic programming (Zuker and Stiegler 1981). The method exploits nesting: the best structure of a segment from nucleotide i to nucleotide j can be built from the best structures of shorter segments, which are computed first and stored. The computing time grows only as the cube of the length of the chain, so that molecules of hundreds of nucleotides can be folded routinely on an ordinary computer.
The same recursions can be used to calculate the sum of exp(−ΔG/RT) over all structures, the partition function Z. The probability of any single structure s is then
\[
p(s) = \frac{\exp(-\Delta G_s / RT)}{Z}
\tag{7.3}\]
where ΔGs is its free energy relative to the unfolded chain. Equation 7.2 is the special case of Equation 7.3 with two states. These calculations are implemented in the ViennaRNA package (Lorenz et al. 2011), used for all folding calculations in this chapter, which applies the Turner 2004 parameters (Mathews et al. 2004).
Predicted structures are models. The energy parameters were measured for short model duplexes and loops, in solutions of defined salt content; tertiary interactions, pseudoknots and bound metal ions are not included. Predictions are most reliable for short molecules with stable helices, and less reliable for long molecules whose function depends on tertiary structure.

title: 7  Folding into Shapes
text:
7.5 From shape to function: ribozymes

Enzymes made of RNA
An enzyme is a biological catalyst (Section 2.8). Until the early 1980s, all known enzymes were proteins. A ribozyme is an RNA molecule that acts as a catalyst. The existence of ribozymes was demonstrated by two independent discoveries.






TipKey experiment: Kruger et al. 1982; Guerrier-Takada et al. 1983



In the ciliate Tetrahymena, the precursor of a ribosomal RNA contains an intervening sequence that must be removed, and the flanking pieces joined, in a process called splicing. The group of Thomas Cech found that the purified precursor RNA, incubated with monovalent and divalent cations and a guanosine factor, spliced itself: the intervening sequence was cut out, with guanosine attached to its 5\('\) end, and the flanking RNA was joined. The authors concluded that “splicing activity is intrinsic to the structure of the RNA, and that enzymes, small nuclear RNAs and folding of the pre-rRNA into an RNP are unnecessary for these reactions” (Kruger et al. 1982).
Ribonuclease P is an enzyme of RNA and protein that cuts the precursors of transfer RNAs. The groups of Sidney Altman and Norman Pace showed that the RNA components of the enzyme from two bacteria, Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis, cleave the precursors on their own in solutions containing 60 mM Mg2+, or 10 mM Mg2+ with 1 mM spermidine. Under these conditions, “the RNA acts as a true catalyst … whereas the protein moieties of the enzymes alone show no catalytic activity”; at lower Mg2+ concentrations without spermidine both subunits were required (Guerrier-Takada et al. 1983).
Altman and Cech received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1989 “for their discovery of catalytic properties of RNA” (Nobel Prize Outreach, n.d.).


Catalysis by RNA depends on folding. A ribozyme positions the reacting groups of its substrate next to each other, and next to bound metal ions or to functional groups of its own nucleotides, so that the transition state (Section 2.8) is stabilised. Only a molecule with a defined three-dimensional structure can do this. A ribozyme is therefore both a sequence, which can in principle be copied, and a folded catalyst. This dual role is the basis of the RNA world hypothesis, introduced in Section 8.1.


In vitro selection
The natural ribozymes were discovered in living cells. In 1990, two groups showed that RNA molecules with a desired property can also be isolated from a large collection of synthetic sequences, by in vitro selection. The procedure has three steps, repeated in cycles:

A pool of RNA molecules is prepared in which part of the sequence is random, so that the pool contains a very large number of different sequences.
The molecules that have the desired property, for example binding to a target molecule fixed on a solid support, are separated from those that do not.
The selected molecules are copied and amplified with enzymes to form the pool for the next cycle.

Because each cycle enriches the pool in active molecules, a few cycles can isolate sequences that were initially extremely rare. RNA molecules selected to bind a specific target are called aptamers.






TipKey experiment: Ellington and Szostak 1990; Tuerk and Gold 1990



Ellington and Szostak isolated, from a population of random-sequence RNA molecules, subpopulations that bind specifically to a variety of organic dyes. They estimated that “roughly one in 1010 random sequence RNA molecules folds in such a way as to create a specific binding site for small ligands” (Ellington and Szostak 1990).
Tuerk and Gold randomised an eight-nucleotide region of an RNA that binds the DNA polymerase of bacteriophage T4, giving a pool of 48 = 65 536 sequences. Cycles of selection for binding and amplification yielded two sequences: the natural sequence, and a variant differing from it at four positions, with equivalent binding constants. The title of their paper names the method: systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment, abbreviated SELEX (Tuerk and Gold 1990).


In vitro selection was soon applied to catalysis. Bartel and Szostak isolated new ribozymes from a large pool of random-sequence RNA. The ribozymes ligate two RNA molecules aligned on a template, by catalysing the attack of a 3\('\)-hydroxy group on an adjacent 5\('\)-triphosphate. This forms a 3\('\),5\('\)-phosphodiester bond, the reaction used by the protein enzymes that synthesise RNA in cells. After further cycles of selection, ribozymes emerged whose reaction rates were 7 million times faster than the uncatalysed reaction (Bartel and Szostak 1993). Ribozymes that join RNA strands are the starting point for the ribozyme polymerases discussed in Section 8.5.

title: 7  Folding into Shapes
text:
7.6 How common is function?

Sequence space
The set of all sequences of a given length is called sequence space. With four nucleotides, there are 4n sequences of length n. For n = 40 this is 440 \(\approx\) 1.2 × 1024, or 2.0 mol of molecules. The mean mass of an RNA residue is about 321 g mol−1 (the mean molar mass of the four nucleoside monophosphates in Table 5.1, 339.5 g mol−1, minus one water molecule, 18.0 g mol−1), so a single copy of every 40-mer would have a mass of about 26 kg. For n = 100, 4100 \(\approx\) 1.6 × 1060. This is far more than the number of atoms in the Earth, which is less than 4 × 1051: that is the number the Earth would contain if its whole mass, 5.9722 × 1024 kg (Section 3.2), were made of hydrogen, the lightest atom, with a mass of 1.67 × 10−27 kg (Section 1.1). Any real population of RNA molecules, whether in a laboratory or on the early Earth, contains only a vanishingly small fraction of sequence space for chains of this length.
The question for the origin of life is therefore not whether a given functional sequence was present, but how many functional sequences there are, and whether a random sample can be expected to contain any of them. A pool of 1015 molecules, for example, corresponds to 1.7 nmol, about 21 \(\mu\)g of 40-mers. If one sequence in 1010 binds a given small molecule, as estimated by Ellington and Szostak (1990), such a pool would contain about 105 binders.


Most random sequences fold
A necessary condition for function is folding. Figure 7.4 shows the MFE structures of random RNA sequences, computed with ViennaRNA at 37 °C (author’s calculation; 4000 sequences each of length 20 and 40, and 2000 of length 80, for each alphabet). With all four nucleotides, 35 percent of random 20-mers have no stable structure, but only 0.9 percent of random 40-mers and none of the 80-mers; the mean MFE is −5.9, −26.4 and −72.5 kJ mol−1 for the three lengths, and about half of the nucleotides of an 80-mer are paired. The structures are also diverse: the 4000 random 40-mers gave 3882 different MFE structures, and the 4000 random 20-mers gave 682.






Figure 7.4: Folding of random RNA sequences at 37 °C, calculated with ViennaRNA and the Turner 2004 parameters (author’s calculation). (a) Distribution of the minimum free energy of 4000 random 40-mers made of four nucleotides, or of only A and U, or of only G and C. (b) Mean fraction of nucleotides paired in the MFE structure as a function of length.



Folding depends strongly on the alphabet. Sequences made only of A and U fold weakly, because A–U stacks are the least stable in Table 7.1: 84 percent of random 20-mers of A and U have no stable structure, and the mean MFE of the 40-mers is only −9.4 kJ mol−1. Sequences made only of G and C fold very strongly (mean MFE of the 40-mers −115.3 kJ mol−1), but they can form many alternative structures of similar stability, and their helices are hard to melt. The four-letter alphabet lies between these extremes.


A ribozyme with two letters
Must a functional RNA contain all four nucleotides? Reader and Joyce used in vitro evolution to obtain ligase ribozymes composed of only two nucleotides, 2,6-diaminopurine and uracil. 2,6-Diaminopurine is an adenine analogue with an additional amino group, which allows it to form three hydrogen bonds with uracil instead of the two of an A–U pair. These ribozymes catalyse the template-directed joining of two RNA molecules, one bearing a 5\('\)-triphosphate and the other a 3\('\)-hydroxy group, and form specifically 3\('\),5\('\)-phosphodiester bonds. The fastest had a catalytic rate about 36 000 times the uncatalysed rate (Reader and Joyce 2002). This is far below the rate enhancement of the four-letter ligases of Bartel and Szostak (1993), but it shows that a binary alphabet can encode catalysis.
These results establish two facts and leave one open question. Established: most random RNA sequences longer than a few tens of nucleotides fold into some structure, and functional sequences, such as binders and ligases, can be isolated from random-sequence pools in the laboratory. Open question: how frequent functional sequences are for the activities that matter most for the origin of life, above all the copying of RNA, and whether the short chains that prebiotic chemistry can make (Section 6.7) are long enough to contain them. Chapter 8 takes up this question.

title: 7  Folding into Shapes
text:
Summary

RNA forms Watson-Crick pairs, A–U (two hydrogen bonds) and G–C (three), and G·U wobble pairs. Paired strands are antiparallel and wind into a right-handed double helix.
Helix stability comes from base stacking as well as pairing. In the nearest-neighbour model the free energy of a helix is the sum of stack terms plus an initiation term; G–C stacks are the most stable (down to −14.2 kJ mol−1 at 37 °C), A–U stacks the least.
The fraction of folded molecules is 1/(1 + exp(ΔG/RT)). Because both ΔH and ΔS of helix formation are negative, helices melt on heating; a four-base-pair hairpin with a UUCG loop melts at about 64 °C.
Secondary structure is the set of nested base pairs, written in dot-bracket notation and composed of helices, hairpin loops, bulges, internal loops, multibranch loops and the exterior loop. The minimum free energy structure is found by dynamic programming.
Ribozymes are catalytic RNA molecules, discovered in self-splicing and in ribonuclease P (Nobel Prize 1989). In vitro selection isolates binders and ribozymes, including RNA ligases, from random-sequence pools.
Sequence space is vast (440 \(\approx\) 1.2 × 1024 sequences of length 40). Most random sequences of 40 or more nucleotides fold; about one in 1010 binds a given small molecule; a ribozyme can be built from only two nucleotides. How common copying activity is remains an open question.

title: 7  Folding into Shapes
text:
Exercises

Write the sequence complementary to 5\('\)-GCAUUG-3\('\) in the 5\('\) to 3\('\) direction. Which base pairs does the duplex contain, and how many hydrogen bonds hold it together?

The hairpin of Figure 7.2 has ΔG = −9.1 kJ mol−1 at 50 °C. Calculate the fraction folded at this temperature with Equation 7.2.

Explain, in terms of enthalpy and entropy, why a helix of two base pairs closed by a hairpin loop does not form at 37 °C.
Write the dot-bracket notation for a 20-nucleotide chain in which nucleotides 1 to 5 pair with 16 to 20 and nucleotides 6 to 15 are unpaired. Which structural element do nucleotides 6 to 15 form?
Which of the following pairs of base pairs are nested and which form a pseudoknot: (2, 10) and (4, 8); (2, 10) and (12, 18); (2, 10) and (6, 15)?

Explain why random sequences made only of A and U fold more weakly than sequences of all four nucleotides, and why the two-letter ribozyme of Reader and Joyce (2002) used 2,6-diaminopurine instead of adenine.
