title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
Learning objectives
After reading this chapter you should be able to:

title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
State the RNA world hypothesis and explain why template-directed copying is central to it.
Describe non-enzymatic template-directed primer extension, the improvements made to it, and its present limits.
Explain the strand-separation problem, and use the melting temperature of a duplex to show how it depends on length and concentration.
Derive the error threshold of a replicating sequence and calculate the longest sequence that a given copying accuracy can maintain.
Describe the main ribozyme polymerases made by in vitro evolution and what they can and cannot yet do.
Explain how selection arises among replicating molecules, with reference to self-sustained replication of RNA enzymes.
Compare measured copying rates with the rates that heredity requires, and list the main open questions.

title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
8.1 Templating

The RNA world
In all known organisms, genetic information is stored in DNA, and most catalysis is carried out by proteins. Each of these two kinds of molecule is made with the help of the other. The discovery of ribozymes (Section 7.5) suggested a way out of this circularity. In Joyce’s words, “there are strong reasons to conclude that DNA- and protein-based life was preceded by a simpler life form based primarily on RNA. This earlier era is referred to as the ‘RNA world’, during which the genetic information resided in the sequence of RNA molecules and the phenotype derived from the catalytic properties of RNA” (Joyce 2002). The term was introduced by Gilbert in 1986 (Gilbert 1986). Orgel regarded the evidence as strong: “The demonstration that ribosomal peptide synthesis is a ribozyme-catalyzed reaction makes it almost certain that there was once an RNA World. The central problem for origin-of-life studies, therefore, is to understand how a protein-free RNA World became established on the primitive Earth” (Orgel 2004).
The RNA world hypothesis is the hypothesis that, at an early stage of life, RNA served both as the genetic material and as the main catalyst. That such a stage existed is a hypothesis with substantial support; how it arose from the chemistry of Chapters 4 to 7 is an open question. Its central requirement is that RNA sequences can be copied.


Copying by complementarity
The rules of base pairing (Section 7.1) provide a copying mechanism. A template is a strand whose sequence directs the order in which nucleotides are joined (Section 5.5). A short strand bound to the template, the primer, is extended at its 3\('\) end: a nucleotide that pairs with the next template base is held in position and joined to the primer (Figure 8.1 a). The product is the complement of the template, not an identical copy. A second round of copying, with the complement as template, restores the original sequence. Replication of a sequence therefore requires two rounds of template-directed synthesis, and between the rounds the product must be separated from its template (Figure 8.1 b).






Figure 8.1: (a) Template-directed primer extension. The primer (blue) is paired with the 3\('\) end of the template (teal); an activated nucleotide that pairs with the next template base is joined to the 3\('\) end of the primer. (b) The copying cycle. Copying produces a duplex of template and complement; only after the two strands are separated can each serve as a template again.

title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
8.2 Non-enzymatic primer extension

What has been achieved
Template-directed synthesis without enzymes was introduced in Section 6.2: activated nucleotides, such as phosphorimidazolides, join on a template in the order specified by base pairing.






TipKey experiment: Inoue and Orgel 1983



Inoue and Orgel showed that templates containing mainly cytidine direct the synthesis of oligonucleotides from mixtures of activated mononucleotides. A nucleotide was incorporated into the products if and only if its complement was present in the template, the reaction had high fidelity, and the products had mean chain lengths of six to ten nucleotides (Inoue and Orgel 1983). The experiment established that sequence information can be transferred by base pairing alone, without enzymes, and that the transfer is selective.


The successful early experiments used templates rich in C, which direct the incorporation of G (Inoue and Orgel 1983). Templates containing A and U are copied far more slowly, by a factor of at least 1000 without helper oligonucleotides (Prywes et al. 2016; Wahiro 2026). Several improvements have been made since.

Better leaving groups. Li and co-workers showed that “activating nucleotides with 2-aminoimidazole results in superior reaction kinetics and improved yields of primer extension reaction products”; among the leaving groups they compared, the rates differed by up to 200 times, with 2-aminoimidazole giving the fastest (Li et al. 2017).
Activated helper oligonucleotides. Prywes and co-workers found that “short 5\('\)-activated oligonucleotides act as catalysts that accelerate primer extension, and allow for the one-pot copying of mixed sequence RNA templates”; with this method they synthesised a significant part of an active hammerhead ribozyme (Prywes et al. 2016).

Chemical self-replication has also been demonstrated with short synthetic templates: in 1986, von Kiedrowski reported a self-replicating hexadeoxynucleotide, a DNA chain of six nucleotides (Kiedrowski 1986).


Present limits
Three limits remain. First, copying is slow: under the most favourable conditions reported, adding one nucleotide takes from tens of minutes to about a day (Section 8.7). Second, an incorrect nucleotide slows further extension. Rajamani and co-workers found “that most mismatches decrease the rate of primer extension by more than 2 orders of magnitude relative to a matched (Watson-Crick) control” (Rajamani et al. 2010). This stalling reduces the number of complete copies that carry errors, but it also wastes time and template. Third, no non-enzymatic system has yet copied a sequence of useful length through repeated cycles of replication. The second round of copying requires the product to be separated from its template, which is the subject of the next section.

title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
8.3 The strand-separation problem

Duplexes are too stable, primers too weak
For a duplex formed from two different strands, each present at total strand concentration CT/2, the melting temperature is the temperature at which half of the strands are paired. It depends on concentration:
\[
T_\mathrm{m} = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ + R \ln (C_\mathrm{T}/4)}
\tag{8.1}\]
where ΔH° and ΔS° are the standard enthalpy and entropy of duplex formation (Section 7.2) and R is the molar gas constant. Because ΔS° is negative and ln(CT/4) is negative for concentrations below 4 mol L−1, lowering the concentration lowers Tm.
Figure 8.2 shows Tm calculated in this way for random RNA duplexes of 4 to 30 base pairs, at total strand concentrations of 1 \(\mu\)M and 1 mM (author’s calculation, with ΔH° and ΔS° from the Turner 2004 parameters in ViennaRNA (Mathews et al. 2004; Lorenz et al. 2011)). At 1 \(\mu\)M, the median melting temperature is −33 °C for 4 base pairs, 17 °C for 6, 41 °C for 8, 56 °C for 10, 85 °C for 20 and 95 °C for 30. At 1 mM, it is 3 °C for 4 base pairs and 44 °C for 6.






Figure 8.2: Melting temperature of random RNA duplexes as a function of length, from Equation 8.1 with nearest-neighbour parameters (Turner 2004, ViennaRNA 2.7.2; author’s calculation, 300 random sequences per length). Lines: median; shaded bands: 10th to 90th percentile; blue, total strand concentration 1 \(\mu\)M; red, 1 mM. Values above 100 °C are extrapolations of the parameter set.



These numbers define the strand-separation problem. Short primers and single nucleotides bind weakly: a primer of 4 to 6 nucleotides stays on its template at ordinary temperatures only at high concentration. The finished product, however, is bound too strongly: a duplex of 20 base pairs or more melts only above about 85 °C at micromolar concentration. A system that copies at low temperature must therefore be heated almost to boiling to release the copy, and at such temperatures RNA is cleaved much faster (Section 6.3). After the strands have separated, they can pair with each other again on cooling, in competition with the primers and monomers that would copy them.


Possible solutions
Several ways around this problem have been proposed; all are hypotheses.

Temperature cycles of short duration, such as those in thermal gradients, could separate strands briefly without prolonged exposure to high temperature.
Lower duplex stability, through changes in salt or pH, or through modified nucleotides that pair more weakly, would lower Tm, at the cost of also weakening primer binding.
Copying with short oligonucleotides rather than single nucleotides joins pieces that bind more strongly, so that copying can take place at higher temperatures, closer to Tm of the product.

None of these has yet produced repeated cycles of non-enzymatic replication of a long sequence.

title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
8.4 Errors and the error threshold

Fidelity
Every copying process makes errors. Let u be the probability that a nucleotide is copied incorrectly, the error rate per nucleotide; q = 1 − u is the fidelity. If errors at different positions are independent, the probability that a sequence of length L is copied without any error is
\[
Q = q^L = (1-u)^L \approx e^{-uL}
\tag{8.2}\]
The approximation holds for small u. The mean number of errors per copy is uL. For example, at u = 0.01, a copy of 100 nucleotides contains on average one error, and only e−1 \(\approx\) 37 percent of copies are error-free.


The error threshold
Consider a population in which one sequence, the master sequence, is replicated \(\sigma\) times faster than all its mutants, and in which mutants rarely mutate back to the master. Only the error-free copies of the master are masters, so the master population grows at a relative rate proportional to \(\sigma\)Q, and all mutants at a rate proportional to 1. The master can persist only if
\[
\sigma Q > 1, \quad \text{that is,} \quad L < \frac{\ln \sigma}{-\ln q} \approx \frac{\ln \sigma}{u}
\tag{8.3}\]
In the steady state its fraction in the population is
\[
x_0 = \frac{\sigma Q - 1}{\sigma - 1}
\tag{8.4}\]
which falls to zero at \(\sigma\)Q = 1. The quantity \(\sigma\) is called the selective superiority of the master. The maximum length Lmax \(\approx\) ln \(\sigma\)/u is the error threshold. Above it, the information of the master sequence is lost in a cloud of mutants, an outcome called the error catastrophe. The concept was introduced by Eigen in his theory of the self-organisation of biological macromolecules (Eigen 1971); the population of a master sequence and its mutants is called a quasispecies.
Figure 8.3 a shows the fraction of the master in a population of sequences of length 50 with \(\sigma\) = 10 (author’s calculation). The full calculation, which includes back-mutation for a four-letter alphabet, agrees with Equation 8.4 to within the width of the line. The master fraction falls to zero at uc = 1 − 10−1/50 = 0.045.






Figure 8.3: The error threshold. (a) Fraction of the master sequence in the steady state for L = 50 and \(\sigma\) = 10, as a function of the error rate per nucleotide; solid line, full calculation with back-mutation (four-letter alphabet); dashed line, Equation 8.4. (b) Maximum length that can be maintained, Lmax = ln \(\sigma\)/u, for \(\sigma\) = 2, 10 and 100; the point marks the error rate of the ribozyme polymerase of Johnston et al. (2001) (author’s calculation).



Because \(\sigma\) enters only through its logarithm, the error threshold depends mainly on the error rate. For \(\sigma\) = 10, an error rate of 0.01 allows sequences of about 230 nucleotides, and an error rate of 0.1 only about 23. A system that maintains a ribozyme of 200 nucleotides with \(\sigma\) = 10 must have u below ln 10/200 \(\approx\) 0.012, that is, fewer than about one error in 90 nucleotides. This is a quantitative statement of the requirement that copying be accurate as well as fast.

title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
8.5 Ribozyme polymerases

Laboratory evolution of RNA polymerases
If RNA was once copied by RNA, an RNA molecule must have catalysed the polymerisation of RNA on an RNA template. No such ribozyme is known in nature. Laboratory evolution, starting from the ligase ribozymes of Bartel and Szostak (1993), has produced ribozymes with this activity.






TipKey experiment: Johnston, Unrau, Lawrence, Glasner and Bartel 2001



Johnston and co-workers engineered a ribozyme that “uses nucleoside triphosphates and the coding information of an RNA template to extend an RNA primer by the successive addition of up to 14 nucleotides—more than a complete turn of an RNA helix”. Its polymerisation was accurate: “when primers extended by 11 nucleotides were cloned and sequenced, 1088 of 1100 sequenced nucleotides matched the template” (Johnston et al. 2001). This corresponds to an error rate of 12/1100 \(\approx\) 0.011 per nucleotide. With \(\sigma\) = 10, Equation 8.3 gives Lmax \(\approx\) 2.30/0.0109 \(\approx\) 211 nucleotides, which exceeds the length of the ribozyme (Figure 8.3 b). The obstacle was not accuracy but the length of the product, far shorter than a ribozyme.


Later work extended the length of the products:

Wochner and co-workers evolved and engineered “an RNA polymerase ribozyme capable of synthesizing RNAs of up to 95 nucleotides in length”, and used it to synthesise an active ribozyme from an RNA template (Wochner et al. 2011).
Attwater, Wochner and Holliger evolved polymerase ribozymes in water-ice. These were “able to synthesise RNA in ices at temperatures as low as −19°C”, and led to “a first polymerase ribozyme capable of catalysing the accurate synthesis of an RNA sequence longer than itself (adding up to 206 nucleotides)” (Attwater, Wochner, and Holliger 2013).
Horning and Joyce obtained a polymerase ribozyme able “to synthesize a variety of complex structured RNAs, including aptamers, ribozymes, and, in low yield, even tRNA”. It amplified “short RNA templates by more than 10,000-fold in an RNA-catalyzed form of the PCR” (Horning and Joyce 2016).
Attwater and co-workers reported RNA-catalysed RNA synthesis on structured templates using trinucleotide triphosphates as substrates (Attwater et al. 2018). Building blocks of three nucleotides bind more strongly than single nucleotides and can copy templates that are folded.

Horning and Joyce concluded: “the two prerequisites of Darwinian life—the replication of genetic information and its conversion into functional molecules—can now be accomplished with RNA in the complete absence of proteins” (Horning and Joyce 2016).


What remains to be done
A ribozyme that copies itself, and its complement, through repeated cycles without human intervention has not yet been made. The polymerase ribozymes are large folded molecules, the products of extensive laboratory evolution and engineering, and they use nucleoside triphosphates or trinucleotide triphosphates as substrates, whose prebiotic availability is uncertain. A folded RNA is also a difficult template, because its own base pairs must be opened before it can be copied; the use of triplet building blocks was one response to this difficulty (Attwater et al. 2018). The gap between these molecules and the short chains of Chapter 6 (Section 6.7) is large.

title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
8.6 Selection

Replication and competition
Replicators grow exponentially when their substrates are not limiting. If a population doubles every td, its size at time t is
\[
N(t) = N_0 \, 2^{t/t_\mathrm{d}}
\tag{8.5}\]
Substrates are always limited eventually. Then different replicators compete for the same substrates, and those that replicate faster, more accurately or for longer increase in frequency at the expense of others. This is natural selection at the molecular level. It requires only three things: replication, variation (introduced by copying errors or recombination) and differences in replication among the variants.






TipKey experiment: Lincoln and Joyce 2009



Lincoln and Joyce converted an RNA ligase ribozyme into a pair of enzymes that “catalyze each other’s synthesis from a total of four oligonucleotide substrates”. These cross-replicating enzymes underwent “self-sustained exponential amplification in the absence of proteins or other biological materials”, with “a doubling time of about 1 hour”, and amplification “can be continued indefinitely”. When populations of different cross-replicating enzymes competed for a common pool of substrates, “recombinant replicators arose and grew to dominate the population” (Lincoln and Joyce 2009).


Each cross-replicating enzyme catalyses the formation of its partner, and so, over two steps, of copies of itself: the system is autocatalytic in the sense of Section 2.8. With a doubling time of 1 hour, Equation 8.5 gives a 224 \(\approx\) 1.7 × 107-fold increase in a day, as long as substrates last. The experiment demonstrates exponential replication and selection among RNA enzymes. In this system, however, the replicators are assembled from four supplied oligonucleotides, so new variants arise by recombination of the supplied pieces, not by copying sequences one nucleotide at a time.

title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
8.7 How fast is fast enough?

A race against loss
A template is useful only if it is copied before it is destroyed. If a template of L nucleotides is copied at r nucleotides per unit time, one copy takes L/r. If the template survives for a mean time \(\tau\), set by hydrolysis (Section 6.3), outflow or adsorption, the mean number of complete copies it can make is about r\(\tau\)/L, and a lineage can persist only if
\[
\frac{r \tau}{L} > 1
\tag{8.6}\]
This inequality is necessary but not sufficient: each copy must also be separated from its template (Section 8.3) and be accurate enough (Section 8.4), and the copies must in turn be copied.


Measured rates against required rates
The author’s own simulations illustrate how strongly the outcome depends on r (Wahiro 2026). That study built a bottom-up model chemistry, from feedstock through activated monomers, chains, catalysts and template copying to vesicles, and searched 13 environmental variables, with ranges taken from the literature, for environments in which heredity arises. Heredity, defined as a sequence lineage that outlives its molecules because it is copied, appeared in a narrow class of cool environments with slow flushing and temperature cycles across the melting temperature of short duplexes.
A later check showed that this result depends on the copying rate. In the model, template-directed extension was about 109 to 1011 times faster than measured non-enzymatic copying, which, with activated nucleotides at 20 to 50 mM and 100 to 200 mM Mg2+, takes from 30 minutes to about a day per added nucleotide even with activated helper oligonucleotides (Prywes et al. 2016; Wahiro 2026). When the extension rate was set to a value anchored in that literature, about one nucleotide per hour, template copying stopped entirely: short duplexes dissociated about 106 times faster than a nucleotide was added. Two other routes, templated ligation of chance oligomers and chance long primers, also failed to start heredity from scratch within the ranges studied. A second, independent limit appeared when the model’s constants were translated into real base pairs with nearest-neighbour parameters: the environments where heredity arose combined the weak pairing of A–U with the accuracy and copying speed found experimentally only for G–C-rich templates, and no measured base pair has both (Wahiro 2026). A supplementary study found, in addition, that heredity at the confirmed points depended in part on a numerical rule of the simulation for sharing out scarce chain slots (Wahiro 2026).
These results are not a proof that heredity cannot arise by non-enzymatic chemistry. They are a quantitative statement of the gap: with measured rates and measured base-pair stabilities, a short template is released from its partner long before it is copied, and nothing in the environments studied closes this gap. A path to heredity therefore needs either copying chemistry many orders of magnitude faster than any yet measured, a mechanism that holds templates and building blocks together for much longer (for example in ice, on surfaces or in compartments), or a first replicator that was not a template copied one nucleotide at a time.

title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
8.8 What remains unknown
The path described in this book, from atoms to self-copying RNA, has been established in parts, not as a whole. The following are open questions, in the order of the chapters.

Feedstock and building blocks. Which environments supplied the nucleotides of Chapters 4 and 5, in sufficient purity and concentration, together with a means of activating them repeatedly?
Homochirality. How did a single handedness of ribose arise and persist (Section 5.5)?
Chains. How were chains of 30 or more nucleotides made in useful amounts, given the competition between polymerisation and hydrolysis (Section 6.7)?
Function. How common are sequences with copying activity among short random sequences (Section 7.6)?
Copying. Can any chemistry, with or without a ribozyme, copy RNA fast and accurately enough, and separate the strands, to sustain repeated cycles of replication (Section 8.3, Section 8.7)?
Selection and compartments. How did replicating sequences become linked to the functions they encode, so that selection could act on them? This question leads to protocells, the subject of the Epilogue.

title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
Summary

The RNA world hypothesis holds that RNA once served as both genetic material and catalyst. It requires that RNA can be copied. Copying by base pairing produces the complement; replication requires two rounds and strand separation.
Non-enzymatic primer extension with activated nucleotides copies sequences selectively. Better leaving groups (2-aminoimidazole) and activated helper oligonucleotides have extended it to mixed sequences, but it remains slow, and mismatches stall extension by more than two orders of magnitude.
Short primers bind weakly and long products bind too strongly: the median Tm of a random 6-base-pair duplex at 1 \(\mu\)M is 17 °C, that of a 20-base-pair duplex 85 °C. This is the strand-separation problem.
A master sequence of length L with selective superiority \(\sigma\) is maintained only if \(\sigma\)(1 − u)L > 1, so that Lmax \(\approx\) ln \(\sigma\)/u. An error rate of 0.01 per nucleotide allows a few hundred nucleotides.
Ribozyme polymerases made in the laboratory extend primers by up to 206 nucleotides, synthesise functional RNAs and amplify RNA exponentially, but none yet replicates itself. Cross-replicating ligases replicate exponentially with a doubling time of about 1 hour and show selection.
Measured non-enzymatic copying is far slower than heredity from scratch requires; in the author’s simulations, heredity appeared only with copying about 109 to 1011 times faster than measured.

title: 8  RNA Copying Itself
text:
Exercises

Write the product of copying the template 5\('\)-GGCAU-3\('\), and the product of copying that product. Why does replication require two rounds of copying?
Explain why non-enzymatic copying of templates rich in C is easier than copying of templates rich in A and U, using the stack free energies of Table 7.1.
A duplex has ΔH° = −250 kJ mol−1 and ΔS° = −0.70 kJ K−1 mol−1. Using Equation 8.1, calculate Tm at CT = 1 \(\mu\)M and at 1 mM.

title: Epilogue: From RNA to Cells
text:
Compartments
This book has followed one chemical path: from the formation of the elements, through small molecules and nucleotides, to chains of RNA that fold, catalyse and, under laboratory conditions, copy other RNA. A self-copying molecule is not yet a living cell. This epilogue outlines the next steps and states where the frontier of knowledge lies.
A replicating molecule in open solution shares its products with every other molecule nearby. A ribozyme that improves replication helps its competitors as much as itself, and selection cannot favour it. Selection for function requires that the products of a sequence stay with that sequence. A compartment, a closed boundary that holds a set of molecules together, provides this link. A compartment that contains a replicating genetic system is called a protocell.
Models of protocell membranes are made from fatty acids: molecules with a carboxylic acid head group (Functional groups) and a long hydrocarbon tail. Such molecules are amphiphilic, having a polar part that interacts favourably with water and a non-polar part that does not. In water, above a critical concentration, they assemble into micelles, small aggregates with the tails inside and the head groups facing the water, or into vesicles: closed membranes, made of a double layer of molecules, that enclose a volume of water. The hydrophobic effect (Forces between molecules) drives this assembly. Fatty acid membranes are simpler than the phospholipid membranes of modern cells, and are more permeable to small molecules.
Laboratory work has shown that such vesicles can carry out several functions of a cell. Hanczyc, Fujikawa and Szostak found that the clay montmorillonite, known to catalyse the polymerisation of RNA (Help from surfaces: montmorillonite), “accelerates the spontaneous conversion of fatty acid micelles into vesicles”; RNA adsorbed to clay can be encapsulated within vesicles; and “once formed, such vesicles can grow by incorporating fatty acid supplied as micelles and can divide without dilution of their contents by extrusion through small pores” (Hanczyc, Fujikawa, and Szostak 2003). Zhu and Szostak described a simpler pathway: large multilamellar vesicles fed with fatty acid micelles grow into long thread-like vesicles, and “modest shear forces are then sufficient to cause the thread-like vesicles to divide into multiple daughter vesicles without loss of internal contents”; encapsulated RNA is distributed to the daughters, and the protocells “can proceed through multiple cycles of reproduction” (Zhu and Szostak 2009).

title: Epilogue: From RNA to Cells
text:
Coupling genome and compartment






TipKey experiment: Chen, Roberts and Szostak 2004



Chen, Roberts and Szostak showed that “RNA, encapsulated in fatty acid vesicles, exerts an osmotic pressure on the vesicle membrane that drives the uptake of additional membrane components, leading to membrane growth at the expense of relaxed vesicles, which shrink.” The authors concluded: “Thus, more efficient RNA replication could cause faster cell growth, leading to the emergence of Darwinian evolution at the cellular level” (Chen, Roberts, and Szostak 2004). The coupling requires no function of the RNA other than its presence, and its replication.


Copying chemistry and membranes must also be compatible. Fatty acid membranes allow small charged molecules, such as nucleotides, to pass, and activated nucleotides added outside a model protocell can cross the membrane and take part in template copying inside it (Mansy et al. 2008). The Mg2+ ions needed for non-enzymatic copying disrupt fatty acid membranes, but Adamala and Szostak found that citrate protects the membranes from high Mg2+ concentrations while allowing RNA copying to proceed (Adamala and Szostak 2013).

title: Epilogue: From RNA to Cells
text:
From RNA to proteins
Modern cells make proteins on the ribosome, a large complex of RNA and protein. The structure of the large ribosomal subunit showed that the site at which peptide bonds are formed consists of RNA: the ribosome is a ribozyme (Nissen et al. 2000). As noted in Templating, Orgel regarded this as making it “almost certain that there was once an RNA World” (Orgel 2004). How an RNA world began to make proteins, how the genetic code arose, and how DNA took over the storage of genetic information are questions beyond the scope of this book.

title: Epilogue: From RNA to Cells
text:
The open frontier
Each chapter of this book has separated what is established from what is hypothesised. The established parts are substantial: the elements of RNA other than hydrogen are made in stars (Chapter 1); its building blocks form in plausible prebiotic reactions (Chapters 4 and 5); activated nucleotides join into chains on minerals and in ice (Chapter 6); random RNA sequences fold, and some of them bind and catalyse (Chapter 7); RNA enzymes made in the laboratory copy RNA and replicate exponentially (Chapter 8); and vesicles grow, divide and compete (this epilogue).
The open questions lie at the joins between these parts. Each step has been demonstrated under its own conditions, often with purified reagents and controlled cycles, and the conditions differ from step to step. No experiment has yet started from simple feedstock and arrived at a replicating, evolving system. The quantitative gaps are largest at copying: measured non-enzymatic copying is far too slow to sustain heredity from scratch (How fast is fast enough?), and laboratory ribozyme polymerases are far longer and more complex than the chains that prebiotic chemistry produces.
A further requirement became clear in the author’s simulations of protocells. Where heredity and vesicles coexisted, vesicle families carrying copied sequences won a single selective sweep, after which copying refilled every vesicle to the same load, and no heritable variation remained for selection to act on (Wahiro 2026). In that model, sustained evolution would need a sequence-dependent trait that copying does not erase, a sequence that does something, for example by catalysing its own copying, building its own membrane or protecting its compartment. This is the link between Chapters 7 and 8 that remains to be found: a sequence that is both copied and useful, in a chemistry and an environment where both happen at once.
The origin of life is therefore not a solved problem. It is a problem whose parts can now be stated precisely, measured in the laboratory and tested in models, which is the condition for solving it.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
This glossary lists the technical terms defined in the book, in alphabetical order. Each entry gives the term, its definition, and the chapter in which it is first used (or the Epilogue).

Terms defined in this book, with the chapter of first use.







Term
Definition
First used




5\('\) to 3\('\) direction
The direction of a nucleic acid chain from the end with a free 5\('\) group to the end with a free 3\('\)-hydroxy group; sequences are written in this direction.
6


Abundance (cosmic)
The relative amount of an element in a defined body or region, expressed as the number of atoms relative to hydrogen or as a mass fraction.
1


Acid
A substance that donates a proton (H+) to another molecule.
2


Activated reactant
A reactant that carries a built-in source of free energy, allowing a condensation to proceed in water.
4


Activation energy (Ea)
The energy barrier that reactants must overcome to react; defined by IUPAC through the temperature dependence of the rate constant, Ea = RT2 d(ln k)/dT.
2


Activity
The effective concentration of a dissolved species, corrected for interactions between particles, expressed relative to a standard concentration of 1 mol per litre.
2


Activity (of water)
The effective concentration of water relative to pure water; it is lowered by evaporation and by concentration of solutes.
5


Addition reaction
A reaction in which two molecules combine to form a single product without the loss of any atoms.
4


Adenine
The purine C5H5N5; formally a pentamer of HCN.
4


Alanine
The amino acid H2NCH(CH3)COOH (R = CH3); \(\beta\)-alanine, H2NCH2CH2COOH, is a structural isomer.
4


Alcohol
A compound in which a hydroxy group, –OH, is attached to a carbon atom that forms only single bonds.
4


Aldehyde
A compound containing the group –CHO, a carbon atom double-bonded to oxygen and bonded to hydrogen.
3


Aldol reaction
Addition of the carbon atom next to the carbonyl group of one molecule, made nucleophilic in basic solution, to the carbonyl carbon of another, forming a carbon-carbon bond.
4


Aldose
A sugar whose carbonyl group is an aldehyde at the end of the carbon chain.
4


Alkaline hydrothermal vent
A hydrothermal vent, not driven directly by volcanic heat, that emits warm, alkaline fluids rich in H2 and CH4, such as the Lost City field.
3


Alpha particle
A helium-4 nucleus, consisting of two protons and two neutrons.
1


Amide
A compound derived from an acid by replacing a hydroxy group with an amino or substituted amino group; in carboxylic amides, –CO–NH2.
4


Amine
A compound containing a nitrogen atom bonded to one or more carbon atoms and carrying a lone pair; the simplest group is the amino group, –NH2.
4


Amino acid
A compound containing an amino group and a carboxy group; in the \(\alpha\)-amino acids of proteins both are attached to the same carbon atom, with general formula H2N–CHR–COOH.
4


Aminonitrile
A compound containing an amino group and a nitrile group on the same carbon atom, RCH(NH2)CN; the intermediate of the Strecker synthesis.
4


2-Aminooxazole
A small heterocycle formed from cyanamide and glycolaldehyde; an intermediate in the synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides by Powner and co-workers.
5


Amphiphilic
Having a polar part that interacts favourably with water and a non-polar part that does not.
Epilogue


Ångström (Å)
A unit of length equal to 10−10 m, convenient for bond lengths.
2


Anhydronucleoside
A nucleoside in which an additional bond links the base to the sugar; an intermediate in the 2009 synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides.
5


Annum (a)
The year as a unit of time in geochronology; multiples are written ka (103 a), Ma (106 a) and Ga (109 a).
3


Anomer
One of two stereoisomers of a ring-form sugar or nucleoside that differ only in the configuration at C1 (\(\alpha\) or \(\beta\)).
5


Antiparallel
Of two paired nucleic acid strands: running in opposite 5\('\) to 3\('\) directions, the arrangement required for base pairing.
7


Apatite
A group of calcium phosphate minerals of low solubility.
3


Aptamer
A nucleic acid molecule, usually obtained by in vitro selection, that binds a specific target molecule.
7


Archean
The second eon of Earth history, from 4031 ± 3 Ma to 2500 Ma.
3


Arrhenius equation
k = A e−Ea/RT: the dependence of a rate constant k on absolute temperature T, with pre-exponential factor A and activation energy Ea.
2


Asymmetric autocatalysis
Autocatalysis in which a chiral product catalyses the formation of itself rather than its enantiomer, so that an enantiomeric excess can be amplified.
4


Atom
The smallest unit of a chemical element: a positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons.
1


Atom ratio
The number of atoms of one element in a sample divided by the number of atoms of another element in the same sample.
1


Atomic mass unit (u)
One twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; equivalent to 931.494 MeV of energy.
1


Atomic number (Z)
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; it defines the element.
1


Autocatalysis
Catalysis of a reaction by one of its own products.
2


Autotroph
An organism that makes its organic matter from CO2.
3


Backbone
The alternating sugar-phosphate chain of a nucleic acid, to which the nucleobases are attached.
6


Bar
A unit of pressure equal to 105 Pa, close to the mean atmospheric pressure at sea level.
3


Base
A substance that accepts a proton (H+) from another molecule.
2


Base pair
Two nucleobases on the same or different strands joined by specific hydrogen bonds.
7


Base stacking
The face-to-face packing of the flat rings of adjacent nucleobases along a helix, stabilised by dispersion forces and the hydrophobic effect.
7


Beta-plus decay
Radioactive decay in which a proton in a nucleus becomes a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino.
1


Big Bang
The model in which the Universe evolved from an extremely hot, dense initial state about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding and cooling since.
1


Big Bang nucleosynthesis
The formation of the lightest nuclei (mainly hydrogen and helium-4, with traces of deuterium, helium-3 and lithium-7) in the first minutes after the Big Bang.
1


Binding energy
The energy required to separate a nucleus completely into its protons and neutrons; equal to the mass difference between the free nucleons and the nucleus, multiplied by c2.
1


Bond angle
The angle between two bonds that share an atom.
2


Bond enthalpy
The enthalpy needed to break one mole of a given bond in molecules in the gas phase; e.g. 436.0 kJ mol−1 for H–H.
2


Bond length
The distance between the nuclei of two atoms joined by a chemical bond.
2


Bond order
The number of electron pairs shared between two bonded atoms: 1 for a single, 2 for a double and 3 for a triple bond.
2


Borate
The anion of boric acid; it forms complexes with sugars that have hydroxy groups on adjacent carbon atoms.
4


Buffer (oxygen)
An assemblage of minerals that fixes the oxygen fugacity at a known value at each temperature, such as iron-wüstite or fayalite-magnetite-quartz.
3


Bulge
A loop between two helices with unpaired nucleotides on one strand only.
7


Calcium-aluminium-rich inclusion (CAI)
A rare component of chondritic meteorites and the oldest dated solid of the solar system, 4.567-4.568 billion years old.
1


Carbonaceous chondrite
A chondrite rich in carbon, often containing a wide variety of organic compounds; the Murchison meteorite is an example.
3


Carbonyl group
A carbon atom double-bonded to an oxygen atom, C=O.
4


Carboxylic acid
A compound containing the carboxy group, –COOH.
4


Catalyst
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without changing its overall standard Gibbs energy change; it is regenerated in the reaction.
2


Chandrasekhar mass
The largest mass that the pressure of electrons can support against gravity in a stellar core; when an iron core exceeds it, the core collapses.
1


Chirality
The property of an object of being non-superposable on its mirror image.
4


Chondrite
A meteorite consisting of unprocessed early solar-system material: CAIs, chondrules and iron-nickel metal in a fine-grained matrix.
1


Chondrule
An abundant, rounded, magnesium- and silicon-rich component of chondritic meteorites, formed up to about 4 million years after CAIs.
1


Clay mineral
A layered silicate formed by the weathering of rocks in water.
6


Closed system (geochronology)
A sample to which no parent or daughter atoms have been added and from which none have been removed since the event being dated.
3


CNO cycle
A cycle of nuclear reactions in which carbon, nitrogen and oxygen nuclei catalyse the conversion of four protons into one helium-4 nucleus; the main stellar source of nitrogen-14.
1


Compartment
A closed boundary that holds a set of molecules together and separates them from their surroundings.
Epilogue


Complementary
Of two sequences: able to form Watson-Crick base pairs along their whole length when aligned antiparallel.
7


Concordant age
A uranium-lead age for which the 238U-206Pb and 235U-207Pb ages agree within uncertainty.
3


Condensation reaction
A reaction in which two reactants (or two sites in one molecule) yield one main product together with water or another small molecule.
4


Continental crust
The outer layer of rock that forms the continents; its upper part is the most accessible region of the solid Earth.
1


Core electrons
The electrons in the inner, completely filled shells of an atom; they are tightly bound and do not take part in bonding.
2


Core-collapse supernova
The explosion of a star of more than about 8 solar masses, triggered by the collapse of its iron core.
1


Cosmic microwave background
Nearly uniform microwave radiation filling the sky, released when the Universe first became transparent at recombination and now cooled to about 2.7 K.
1


Covalent bond
A chemical bond formed by a pair of electrons shared between two atoms.
2


Cyanamide
H2NCN, an amino group bonded to a nitrile group; a prebiotic feedstock molecule.
3


Cyanoacetylene
HC\(\equiv\)C–C\(\equiv\)N, a product of spark discharge in CH4/N2 mixtures and a precursor of pyrimidines.
4


Cyanohydrin
A compound in which a hydroxy group and a nitrile group are attached to the same carbon atom, formed by addition of HCN to a carbonyl group.
4


2\('\),3\('\)-Cyclic phosphate
A nucleotide in which one phosphate bridges C2\('\) and C3\('\) in a five-membered ring; an activated form that can form phosphodiester bonds.
5


Cytosine
The pyrimidine C4H5N3O; it is converted to uracil by hydrolysis.
4


Daughter (nuclide)
The nuclide formed by the radioactive decay of a parent nuclide.
3


Debye (D)
The customary unit of molecular dipole moment; 1 D = 3.335 64 × 10−30 C m.
2


Decay (radioactive)
The spontaneous transformation of an unstable nucleus into a different nucleus, with emission of radiation.
1


Decay constant (\(\lambda\))
The probability per unit time that a nucleus of a given radioactive nuclide decays; related to the half-life by t1/2 = ln 2/\(\lambda\).
3


Delta notation (\(\delta\))
The deviation of an isotope ratio in a sample from that of a standard, (\(R\)sample/\(R\)standard − 1) × 1000, expressed in per mil (‰).
3


Detrital
Describes a mineral grain eroded from its original rock and incorporated into a sediment.
3


Deuterium bottleneck
The delay in Big Bang nucleosynthesis caused by the destruction of newly formed deuterons by energetic photons, lasting until the Universe cooled to about 109 K.
1


Deuteron
The nucleus of deuterium, consisting of one proton and one neutron.
1


Diamidophosphate (DAP)
PO2(NH2)2−, a phosphorylating agent that acts in water without an additional condensing agent.
4


Diaminomaleonitrile (DAMN)
The tetramer of HCN, an intermediate in the formation of adenine from HCN.
4


Differentiation (planetary)
The melting of a planetary body and its internal separation into layers, such as a metallic core and a rocky mantle.
1


Dipole moment (\(\mu\))
For charges +q and −q separated by a distance d, the product \(\mu = qd\); a measure of the separation of charge in a molecule.
2


Dipole-dipole interaction
The attraction between the positive end of one polar molecule and the negative end of another.
2


Dispersion force
A weak attraction between temporary, mutually induced dipoles in neighbouring atoms or molecules; it acts between all molecules and grows with molecular size.
2


Dot-bracket notation
A notation for nested secondary structure: a string with a bracket for each paired nucleotide (opening for the 5\('\) partner, closing for the 3\('\) partner) and a dot for each unpaired nucleotide.
7


Double bond
A covalent bond in which two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
2


Double helix
The right-handed helical structure formed by two antiparallel, base-paired nucleic acid strands or segments.
7


Doubling time (td)
The time in which an exponentially growing population doubles in size.
8


Dry mass
The mass of biological material remaining after all water has been removed.
1


Duplex
A complex of two separate nucleic acid strands held together by base pairs.
7


Dynamic programming
A method that solves a problem by combining stored solutions of smaller sub-problems; used to find minimum free energy RNA structures.
7


Electrical discharge
The passage of electric current through a gas, as in lightning, which heats the gas and breaks its molecules into fragments.
3


Electron
A subatomic particle with one negative elementary charge; electrons occupy orbitals around the nucleus and determine chemical behaviour.
1


Electron configuration
A list of the number of electrons in each subshell of an atom, such as 1s2 2s2 2p2 for carbon.
2


Electronegativity (\(\chi\))
A measure of the tendency of an atom in a bond to attract the shared electrons towards itself; on the Pauling scale, H 2.20, C 2.55, N 3.04, O 3.44, P 2.19.
2


Electronvolt (eV)
The energy gained by a particle with one elementary charge moving through a potential difference of one volt; exactly 1.602 176 634 × 10−19 J.
2


Electrophile
A reagent that forms a bond by accepting both bonding electrons from its reaction partner.
4


Element
A substance consisting of atoms that all have the same atomic number.
1


Enantiomeric cross-inhibition
Inhibition of template-directed chain growth by monomers of the opposite handedness, which are incorporated and block further extension.
5


Enantiomeric excess (ee)
([L] − [D])/([L] + [D]), the fractional excess of one enantiomer in a mixture; 0 for a racemate, ±1 for a homochiral sample.
4


Enantiomers
Two molecules that are non-superposable mirror images of each other.
4


Endothermic
Describes a process that absorbs heat from its surroundings (ΔH > 0).
2


Energy level
One of the discrete values of energy that an electron in an atom or molecule can have.
2


Enthalpy (H)
Internal energy of a system plus the product of its pressure and volume; its change equals the heat exchanged at constant pressure.
2


Entropy (S)
A thermodynamic quantity measuring the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with the macroscopic state of a system.
2


Enzyme
A biological catalyst; a protein or, in the case of a ribozyme, an RNA molecule.
7


Eon
The largest unit of geological time; Earth history is divided into the Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic eons.
3


Equilibrium (chemical)
The state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates, so that the amounts of reactants and products no longer change.
2


Equilibrium constant (K)
The ratio, at equilibrium, of the activities of products to those of reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient; related to \(\Delta G^\circ\) by \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K\).
4


Error catastrophe
The loss of the information of a master sequence among its mutants when the error rate exceeds the error threshold.
8


Error rate per nucleotide (u)
The probability that a nucleotide is copied incorrectly; the fidelity is q = 1 − u.
8


Error threshold
The greatest sequence length, Lmax \(\approx\) ln \(\sigma\)/u, that can be maintained by replication with error rate u and selective superiority \(\sigma\).
8


Ester
A compound formally derived from an acid and an alcohol by linking them with the loss of water.
4


Eutectic phase
The concentrated liquid that remains between ice crystals when a solution is cooled below its freezing point.
6


Excited state
A state of a nucleus, atom or molecule with more energy than its lowest-energy state.
1


Exogenous delivery
The arrival on the Earth of organic molecules already present in extraterrestrial objects.
3


Exothermic
Describes a process that releases heat to its surroundings (ΔH < 0).
2


Exterior loop
The unpaired nucleotides of a secondary structure that are not enclosed by any base pair, including the two chain ends.
7


Faint young Sun problem
The difficulty of reconciling the lower luminosity of the young Sun, about 30 percent below the present value, with evidence for liquid water on the early Earth.
3


Fatty acid
A carboxylic acid with a long hydrocarbon chain; an amphiphilic molecule used in models of protocell membranes.
Epilogue


Feedstock molecule
A small, simple molecule from which more complex molecules can be built in a sequence of reactions.
3


Fidelity (q)
The probability that a nucleotide is copied correctly.
8


Formaldehyde
H2CO, the simplest aldehyde; the feedstock of the formose reaction.
3


Formamide
HCONH2, the amide of formic acid; a liquid from 2.6 °C to about 211 °C, from which nucleobases form on heating with mineral catalysts.
4


Formamidopyrimidine
A pyrimidine carrying a formamido group, whose atoms can close a second ring to give a purine; an intermediate in prebiotic purine nucleoside syntheses.
5


Formose reaction
The conversion of formaldehyde, in the presence of a base, into a mixture of sugars; it is autocatalytic.
3


Freeze-out
The point at which a reaction becomes too slow, relative to the expansion of the Universe, to keep the amounts of its products in equilibrium.
1


Functional group
An atom or group of atoms that has similar chemical properties whenever it occurs in different compounds.
4


Furanose
The five-membered ring form of a sugar (four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom), formed by addition of a hydroxy group to the carbonyl group of the same molecule.
4


G\(\cdot\)U wobble pair
A base pair between guanine and uracil held by two hydrogen bonds, with the bases shifted relative to a Watson-Crick pair; common in RNA helices.
7


Gamma ray (\(\gamma\))
A photon of very high energy, typically emitted in nuclear reactions.
1


Geometric distribution
The distribution P(n) = (1 − p)pn−1 of chain lengths when each extension succeeds with probability p; its mean is 1/(1 − p).
6


Giant impact hypothesis
The hypothesis that the Moon formed from debris thrown into orbit when a body about the size of Mars collided with the proto-Earth.
3


Gibbs free energy (G)
G = H - TS. At constant temperature and pressure, a process occurs spontaneously only if it lowers G.
2


Glycine
The simplest amino acid, H2NCH2COOH (R = H); the only common amino acid without a stereocentre.
4


Graphite
A crystalline form of pure carbon.
3


Ground state
The lowest-energy state of a nucleus, atom or molecule.
1


Guanine
The purine C5H5N5O.
4


Hadean
The first eon of Earth history, from the formation of the solar system to 4031 ± 3 Ma.
3


Hairpin loop
A loop of unpaired nucleotides closed by a single base pair at the end of a helix; it contains at least three nucleotides.
7


Half-life
The time required for half of the nuclei in a sample of a radioactive isotope to decay.
1


Helioseismology
The study of the interior of the Sun through its oscillations, observed at its surface.
1


Helium burning
Nuclear fusion of helium in a stellar core, producing mainly carbon-12 and oxygen-16; it requires temperatures near 108 K.
1


Helium mass fraction (Y)
The fraction of the total mass of ordinary matter that is in the form of helium-4.
1


Helix (stem)
In secondary structure, a run of consecutive stacked base pairs.
7


Hess’s law
The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken, so it can be calculated from tabulated enthalpies of formation.
2


Heterocyclic compound
A cyclic compound whose ring contains atoms of at least one element other than carbon.
4


Homochirality
The property of consisting of only one of two enantiomers, as RNA consists only of D-ribose units.
4


Hoyle state
The excited state of carbon-12 at 7.65 MeV, through which the triple-alpha process proceeds.
1


Hund’s rule
In a partly filled subshell, electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before any orbital receives a second electron.
2


Hybridisation
The description of a bonded atom’s valence orbitals as mixtures of its s and p orbitals (sp3, sp2, sp) that point in the directions of its bonds.
2


Hydration shell
The layer of oriented water molecules surrounding a dissolved ion or molecule.
2


Hydrogen bond
An attractive interaction between a hydrogen atom of a group X–H, in which X is more electronegative than H, and an atom or group of atoms in the same or another molecule, in which there is evidence of bond formation (IUPAC 2011); written X–H···Y.
2


Hydrogen burning
Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in a star; a nuclear, not a chemical, process.
1


Hydrogen cyanide
HCN, a linear molecule with a carbon-nitrogen triple bond; a feedstock for nucleobases.
3


Hydrogen-bond acceptor
The atom Y, usually O or N with a lone pair, that receives a hydrogen bond X–H···Y.
2


Hydrogen-bond donor
The atom X to which the hydrogen of a hydrogen bond X–H···Y is covalently bonded.
2


Hydrolysis
The breaking of a bond by reaction with water; the reverse of a condensation.
4


Hydronium ion
The ion H3O+, formed when a water molecule accepts a proton.
2


Hydrophilic
Interacting favourably with water; describes polar and charged molecules or groups.
2


Hydrophobic effect
The tendency of non-polar molecules or groups to cluster together in water, reducing their contact with water.
2


Hydrothermal vent
A site on the sea floor where water heated within the crust flows out into the ocean.
3


Hydroxide ion
The ion OH−, formed when a water molecule loses a proton.
2


Imidazole
A five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms, C3H4N2.
6


Imine
A compound containing a carbon-nitrogen double bond, R2C=NR; formed by condensation of an aldehyde or ketone with ammonia or an amine.
4


Impact-shock synthesis
The formation of organic molecules by shock heating during the entry or impact of extraterrestrial objects.
3


In vitro selection
Repeated cycles of selecting molecules with a desired property from a pool of random sequences and amplifying them.
7


Intermolecular force
An attraction between molecules, much weaker than a covalent bond, such as dipole-dipole, dispersion and hydrogen-bond interactions.
2


Internal loop
A loop between two helices with unpaired nucleotides on both strands.
7


Interplanetary dust particle (IDP)
A small particle of extraterrestrial dust that falls on the Earth from space.
3


Ion
An atom or molecule with a net electric charge, resulting from an unequal number of protons and electrons.
1


Ion product of water (Kw)
The product of the activities of H3O+ and OH− in water at equilibrium; pKw = 13.99 at 25 °C.
2


Ionic bond
A bond formed by the electrostatic attraction between ions of opposite charge, resulting from the transfer of electrons between atoms of very different electronegativity.
2


Ionisation energy (first)
The minimum energy required to remove one electron from a neutral atom in its ground state.
2


Isomers
Species with the same molecular formula but different structures.
4


Isotope
Atoms of the same element (same atomic number) that differ in their number of neutrons.
1


Isotope fractionation
The partial separation of isotopes of different mass by physical or chemical processes.
3


Ketone
A compound in which a carbonyl group is bonded to two carbon atoms.
4


Ketose
A sugar whose carbonyl group is a ketone.
4


Late Heavy Bombardment
Impacts on the planets and the Moon after their outer layers became rigid enough to preserve craters and basins; in particular, an episode of elevated impact rate between about 4.2 to 4.0 Ga and 3.5 Ga.
3


Late veneer
Material accreted by the Earth after the Moon-forming impact.
3


Lead-lead age
An age calculated from the ratio of radiogenic 207Pb to radiogenic 206Pb, which depends on the time elapsed but not on the amount of uranium in the sample.
3


Leaving group
The group that departs with an electron pair when a nucleophile attacks; a good leaving group makes the reaction easier.
6


Lewis structure
A diagram of a molecule in which shared electron pairs are drawn as lines and lone pairs as pairs of dots.
2


Log epsilon (log \(\varepsilon\))
An abundance scale defined as log10(NX/NH) + 12, where NX and NH are the numbers of atoms of element X and of hydrogen; hydrogen has 12 by definition.
1


Lone pair
A pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom and is not shared in a bond.
2


Luminosity
The total power emitted by a star, integrated over all wavelengths; the present luminosity of the Sun is 3.85 × 1026 W.
3


Magma ocean
A global layer of molten rock at the surface of a planet or moon.
3


Mass fraction
The mass of one component of a sample divided by the total mass of the sample.
1


Mass number (A)
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.
1


Master sequence
In quasispecies theory, the sequence that replicates fastest; its mutants replicate more slowly.
8


Melting temperature (Tm)
The temperature at which half of the molecules are folded or paired; in the two-state model Tm = \(\Delta\)H/\(\Delta\)S.
7


Meteorite
An extraterrestrial body that survives passage through the atmosphere and reaches the ground.
3


Micelle
A small aggregate of amphiphilic molecules in water, with the non-polar parts inside and the polar parts facing the water.
Epilogue


Minimum free energy (MFE) structure
The secondary structure of lowest Gibbs energy that a sequence can form under a given energy model.
7


Molal (mol kg−1)
A concentration expressed as moles of solute per kilogram of solvent.
3


Molar (M)
A concentration expressed as moles of solute per litre of solution.
3


Mole
The amount of substance containing exactly 6.022 140 76 × 1023 elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions).
2


Molecular cloud
A cold, dense cloud of interstellar gas, in which hydrogen is present mainly as H2 molecules, together with dust; stars form in such clouds.
1


Molecule
Two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds and acting as a single unit.
2


Monoisotopic element
An element that has only one stable isotope, such as phosphorus (31P).
1


Monosaccharide (sugar)
A compound Cn(H2O)n, usually with n from 3 to 7, containing one carbonyl group and a hydroxy group on each other carbon atom.
4


Montmorillonite
A layered clay mineral whose negatively charged aluminium silicate layers adsorb organic molecules; it catalyses the oligomerisation of activated nucleotides.
6


Multibranch loop
A loop from which three or more helices radiate; also called a junction.
7


N-glycosidic bond
The bond between C1\('\) of the sugar and a ring nitrogen of the base (N9 in purines, N1 in pyrimidines) in a nucleoside.
5


Natural selection
The increase in frequency of variants that replicate faster, more accurately or for longer, among replicators competing for limited resources.
8


Nearest-neighbour model
An energy model in which the Gibbs energy of a helix is the sum of terms for each pair of adjacent base pairs plus an initiation term.
7


Neutral atmosphere
An atmosphere in which carbon and nitrogen are present mainly as CO2 and N2, without much H2 or free O2.
3


Neutrino
An electrically neutral elementary particle of very small mass that interacts only weakly with matter.
1


Neutron
An electrically neutral subatomic particle found in the nucleus.
1


Nitrile
A compound containing the group –C\(\equiv\)N.
4


Nuclear fusion
A nuclear reaction in which two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus. For nuclei lighter than iron, fusion releases energy.
1


Nucleobase
A nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compound that, bonded to ribose, forms part of a nucleotide; in RNA, adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil.
4


Nucleon
A proton or a neutron.
1


Nucleophile
A reagent that forms a bond by donating an electron pair to its reaction partner.
4


Nucleoside
A nucleobase joined to a sugar (ribose in RNA), without a phosphate group.
3


Nucleosynthesis
The formation of atomic nuclei by nuclear reactions.
1


Nucleotide
A nucleoside carrying one or more phosphate groups, usually on C5\('\) of the sugar; the monomer unit of RNA.
5


Nucleus (atomic)
The small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
1


Octet rule
The tendency of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen to form bonds until each has eight valence electrons, the configuration of neon.
2


Oligonucleotide
A short chain of nucleotides, often described by its length, as in a 10-mer; a long chain is a polynucleotide.
6


Orbital
A region around a nucleus, described by a wavefunction, in which an electron of a given energy is likely to be found; each orbital holds at most two electrons.
2


Oxidation
The loss of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule; an increase in oxidation number.
3


Oxidation number
The charge an atom would carry if the shared electrons of each of its covalent bonds were assigned to the more electronegative atom.
3


Oxygen fugacity
The effective pressure of O2 in equilibrium with a magma or other system; a measure of how oxidising it is.
3


Parent (nuclide)
A radioactive nuclide that decays into a daughter nuclide.
3


Partition function (Z)
The sum of exp(\(-\Delta\)G/RT) over all structures of a molecule; the probability of a structure is its term divided by Z.
7


Pauli exclusion principle
No two electrons in an atom can be in the same quantum state; hence an orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins.
2


Pentose
A sugar with five carbon atoms; ribose is an aldopentose.
4


Per mil (‰)
Parts per thousand.
3


pH
The negative base-10 logarithm of the activity of hydronium ions in a solution; neutral pH equals pKw/2, which is 7.00 at 25 °C.
2


Phosphate
The ion PO43−, in which phosphorus is bonded tetrahedrally to four oxygen atoms; also used for groups derived from it.
3


Phosphate ester
An ester formed from phosphoric acid and an alcohol; the units of RNA are joined by phosphate ester linkages.
4


Phosphate problem
The mismatch between the low concentrations of phosphate in natural waters and the high concentrations used in prebiotic experiments.
3


Phosphoanhydride bond
A P–O–P linkage formed by condensation of two phosphate groups, as in pyrophosphate and ATP; its hydrolysis releases more free energy than that of a phosphate ester.
4


Phosphodiester bond
The phosphate diester linkage that joins the C3 hydroxy group of one ribose to the C5 hydroxy group of the next in RNA.
4


Phosphoric acid
H3PO4, a triprotic acid; its anions are collectively called phosphate.
4


Phosphorimidazolide
A nucleotide in which one oxygen of the phosphate is replaced by a nitrogen atom of imidazole or a substituted imidazole; an activated monomer.
6


Phosphorylation
The attachment of a phosphate group to a molecule.
4


Photochemistry
Chemical reactions initiated by the absorption of light.
3


Photosphere
The layer of a star from which its visible light escapes into space; stellar abundances are measured from absorption lines formed there.
1


Phytoplankton
Microscopic photosynthetic organisms living in the surface waters of oceans and lakes.
1


Pi (\(\pi\)) bond
A covalent bond formed by side-by-side overlap of two parallel p orbitals, with electron density above and below the line joining the nuclei.
2


Plasma
A gas in which a significant fraction of atoms are ionised, so that it contains free electrons and positively charged nuclei or ions.
1


Polar bond
A covalent bond in which the shared electrons are unequally distributed because the two atoms differ in electronegativity; the ends carry partial charges \(\delta+\) and \(\delta-\).
2


Polar molecule
A molecule with a net dipole moment, because the dipoles of its polar bonds do not cancel.
2


Polyphosphate
A chain or ring of phosphate units joined by phosphoanhydride bonds, such as pyrophosphate or trimetaphosphate.
4


Positron
The antiparticle of the electron, with the same mass and opposite (positive) charge.
1


Primer
A short strand bound to a template and extended at its 3\('\) end during copying.
8


Principal quantum number (n)
The number (1, 2, 3, …) that labels an electron shell; higher n means electrons that are on average farther from the nucleus.
2


Protocell
A compartment, such as a vesicle, that contains a replicating genetic system; a model of an early cell.
Epilogue


Proton
A subatomic particle with one positive elementary charge, found in the nucleus.
1


Proton-proton chain
The sequence of fusion reactions that converts four protons into one helium-4 nucleus, two positrons and two neutrinos; the main energy source of the Sun.
1


Protoplanetary disc
A flattened, rotating disc of gas and dust around a young star, from which planets form.
1


Pseudoknot
A structure containing base pairs that cross rather than nest: pairs (i, j) and (k, l) with i < k < j < l.
7


Purine
A nucleobase with a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring, nine ring atoms of which four are nitrogen; adenine and guanine.
4


Pyranose
The six-membered ring form of a sugar (five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom).
4


Pyrimidine
A nucleobase with a single six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms; cytosine and uracil (thymine in DNA).
4


Quantum mechanics
The physical theory that describes the behaviour of matter and energy on the scale of atoms and subatomic particles.
2


Quasispecies
The population formed by a master sequence and the mutants generated by its error-prone replication.
8


Racemate
A mixture containing equal amounts of two enantiomers.
4


Radiogenic
Produced by radioactive decay; used of daughter atoms formed within a sample.
3


Radiometric age
The age of a sample calculated from the measured ratio of radiogenic daughter to parent atoms and the decay constant of the parent.
3


Rate constant (k)
The proportionality factor between the rate of a reaction and the concentrations of its reactants; it depends on temperature but not on concentration.
2


Rate of reaction
The rate of change of the concentration of a reactant or product with time, divided by its coefficient in the reaction equation.
2


Recombination
The epoch, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when electrons first bound permanently to nuclei to form neutral atoms.
1


Redfield ratio
The average atom ratio C:N:P = 106:16:1 used as a reference for the composition of marine organisms.
1


Redox couple
A reducing and an oxidising substance that can react with each other by electron transfer, such as H2 and CO2.
3


Redox reaction
A reaction in which one species is oxidised and another reduced.
3


Reducing atmosphere
An atmosphere in which carbon and nitrogen are present mainly in low oxidation states, as CH4 and NH3, together with H2.
3


Reduction
The gain of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule; a decrease in oxidation number.
3


Relative atomic mass (Ar)
The average mass of the atoms of an element in a given sample, expressed in atomic mass units; the standard atomic weight is its recommended value for normal materials.
1


Relative permittivity (\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}\))
The factor by which a medium reduces the electrostatic force between charges compared with a vacuum; 78.4 for water at 25 °C.
2


Replication
The production of a copy of a sequence; for nucleic acids, two rounds of template-directed synthesis separated by strand separation.
8


Resonance (nuclear)
A strong enhancement of a nuclear reaction rate when the energy of the colliding nuclei matches the energy of an excited state of the product nucleus.
1


Ribose
The aldopentose C5H10O5 of RNA; RNA contains only D-ribose, in the furanose form.
4


Ribosome
The complex of RNA and protein on which cells make proteins; its peptide-bond-forming site consists of RNA.
Epilogue


Ribozyme
An RNA molecule that acts as a catalyst.
7


Ribozyme polymerase
A ribozyme that extends an RNA primer on an RNA template; so far obtained only by laboratory evolution.
8


RNA world hypothesis
The hypothesis that, at an early stage of life, RNA served both as genetic material and as the main catalyst.
8


Schreibersite
The meteoritic mineral (Fe,Ni)3P, in which phosphorus is bonded to metal atoms; it releases reactive phosphorus compounds when it corrodes in water.
3


Second law of thermodynamics
In any spontaneous process, the total entropy of a system and its surroundings increases.
2


Secondary structure
The set of base pairs formed by a nucleic acid molecule.
7


Selective superiority (\(\sigma\))
The ratio of the replication rate of the master sequence to that of its mutants.
8


Selectivity
The extent to which a reaction or process forms one product, or acts on one compound, in preference to others.
4


SELEX
Systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment: the in vitro selection procedure of Tuerk and Gold (1990).
7


Sequence space
The set of all sequences of a given length; for RNA of length n it contains 4n sequences.
7


Shell (electron)
The set of orbitals in an atom with the same principal quantum number n; it holds at most 2n2 electrons.
2


Short-lived radionuclide
A radioactive isotope with a half-life of less than 200 million years that was present in the early solar system and is now extinct.
1


Sigma (\(\sigma\)) bond
A covalent bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals, with electron density concentrated along the line joining the nuclei.
2


Snow line
The distance from a young star beyond which ice of a given substance can form; for water the corresponding temperature is about 150 K.
1


Spark discharge experiment
A laboratory simulation in which an electric discharge acts on a gas mixture in contact with water, as in the experiment of Miller (1953).
4


Spin
An intrinsic property of the electron that can take one of two values, conventionally called up and down.
2


Splicing
The removal of an intervening sequence from an RNA precursor and the joining of the flanking pieces.
7


Stack
In the nearest-neighbour model, a pair of adjacent base pairs in a helix.
7


Stalling
The slowing of primer extension after a mismatched nucleotide has been incorporated.
8


Standard enthalpy of formation (ΔfH°)
The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their most stable forms, all in their standard states.
2


Star
A self-gravitating ball of gas in which nuclear fusion in the core supplies the energy radiated from the surface.
1


Stereocentre
An atom, usually carbon bonded to four different groups, at which exchanging two groups gives a stereoisomer.
4


Strand-separation problem
The difficulty that the product of template copying is bound to its template more strongly than primers and monomers, so that releasing it requires conditions that damage RNA.
8


Strecker synthesis
Formation of an amino acid from an aldehyde, ammonia and hydrogen cyanide, through an imine and an aminonitrile that is then hydrolysed.
4


Strong nuclear force
The fundamental force that binds protons and neutrons together in a nucleus; it is much stronger than the electrical repulsion between protons but acts only over distances of about 10−15 m.
1


Structural isomers
Isomers that differ in the order in which their atoms are bonded.
4


Subshell
A group of orbitals within a shell with the same shape, labelled s, p, d or f and containing 1, 3, 5 or 7 orbitals.
2


Supernova
The explosive death of a star, which ejects newly synthesised elements into interstellar space.
1


Supernova remnant
The expanding cloud of gas ejected by a supernova explosion, together with the interstellar gas it sweeps up.
1


Template
An existing nucleotide chain whose sequence directs the order in which monomers are joined.
5


Tertiary structure
The three-dimensional arrangement of the atoms of a folded molecule.
7


Tetrahedral angle
The angle between lines from the centre of a regular tetrahedron to two of its corners, arccos(−1/3), approximately 109.47°.
2


Transition state
The arrangement of atoms at the point of highest energy along the path from reactants to products.
2


Triple bond
A covalent bond in which two atoms share three pairs of electrons.
2


Triple-alpha process
The fusion of three helium-4 nuclei into carbon-12 inside stars, proceeding via unstable beryllium-8.
1


Ultraviolet light
Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths shorter than those of visible light, below about 400 nm.
3


Uracil
The pyrimidine C4H4N2O2; it pairs with adenine in RNA.
4


Valence
The number of covalent bonds an atom usually forms: 1 for H, 4 for C, 3 for N and 2 for O.
2


Valence electrons
The electrons in the outermost shell of an atom, which take part in chemical bonding.
2


Van der Waals forces
The collective name for dipole-dipole, dipole-induced dipole and dispersion interactions between molecules.
2


Vesicle
A closed membrane, made of a double layer of amphiphilic molecules, that encloses a volume of water.
Epilogue


VSEPR
Valence-shell electron-pair repulsion: a model in which the electron pairs around an atom arrange themselves as far apart as possible, determining molecular shape.
2


Watson-Crick base pair
The base pairs A–U (A–T in DNA), with two hydrogen bonds, and G–C, with three.
7


Wet-dry cycle
Repeated drying and rewetting of a small body of water, which concentrates dissolved molecules and promotes the joining of building blocks into chains.
3


Zircon
The mineral zirconium silicate, ZrSiO4; it contains trace uranium, resists weathering, and is the main source of information about the Hadean Earth.
3

title: Appendix C — How to Read a Scientific Paper
text:
C.1 Kinds of publication
Every key experiment in this book is taken from a published research paper, and every claim is linked to its source in the References. This appendix describes how such papers are organised and how to read them critically.
Each publication is identified by a digital object identifier (DOI), a persistent string such as 10.1126/science.1060786. Prefixing it with https://doi.org/ gives a link that resolves to the publication. The DOIs of the works cited in this book are listed in the References.
crumbs: C  How to Read a Scientific Paper

title: Appendix C — How to Read a Scientific Paper
text:
A research article reports new results: an experiment, an observation, a calculation or a model. It is the primary source for a claim.
A review summarises and evaluates the research articles on a topic. Reviews are the best entry point into an unfamiliar field, but a number quoted in a review should be checked in the research article it cites.
A preprint is a manuscript made public before, or without, formal peer review, on a server such as arXiv, bioRxiv or Zenodo.
Peer review is the evaluation of a manuscript by independent experts before publication in a journal. It reduces errors but does not guarantee that a result is correct; the test of a result is whether other laboratories can reproduce it.
crumbs: C  How to Read a Scientific Paper

title: Appendix C — How to Read a Scientific Paper
section: C.2 The structure of a research article
text:
C.2 The structure of a research article
Most research articles in chemistry and biology follow the same order:

Title and abstract. The abstract states the question, the approach, the main result and its significance, usually in a single paragraph. It is the part of a paper most often quoted, and the key experiment boxes of this book quote abstracts directly wherever possible.
Introduction. The background, the open problem and the aim of the work.
Methods (or Materials and Methods, sometimes placed at the end or in supplementary material). The exact conditions: concentrations, temperatures, pH, times, instruments and analysis. Whether a result is relevant to the early Earth often depends on these details.
Results. The observations, usually organised around figures and tables.
Discussion. The interpretation of the results, their limitations and their relation to earlier work.
References and supplementary information, which often contain the full data.
crumbs: C  How to Read a Scientific Paper

title: Appendix C — How to Read a Scientific Paper
text:
C.3 Reading critically
A paper is not read once from beginning to end. A practical order is: title and abstract, then the figures and their legends, then the results and methods for the parts that matter, and finally the discussion. The following questions help to evaluate a claim.

What exactly was measured? Distinguish the observation (for example, the products detected after a reaction) from the interpretation (for example, the mechanism proposed for their formation).
Under what conditions? Concentrations, temperature, pH, purity of reagents and duration determine whether a result could apply to a natural environment. Many experiments in Chapters 4 to 8 use concentrations or purified starting materials that are chosen to make a single step work.
How large is the effect, and how certain? Look for the numbers, their units and their uncertainties. A rate enhancement of 36 000 and one of 7 million (Section 7.6, Section 7.5) are both catalysis, but they differ by more than two orders of magnitude.
What controls were run? A control is an experiment identical to the main one except for the factor under test, such as a reaction without the template or without the catalyst. Without controls, an effect cannot be attributed to its proposed cause.
Has the result been reproduced? Results confirmed by independent groups are more secure than single reports.
Do the conclusions follow from the data? A statement in the discussion may go beyond the results; the abstract may state the most favourable interpretation.
crumbs: C  How to Read a Scientific Paper

title: Appendix C — How to Read a Scientific Paper
text:
C.4 Established, hypothesis, open question
The book distinguishes three kinds of statement, as described in the Preface. When reading a paper, the same distinction is useful:

A result is established when it rests on reproducible measurements under stated conditions.
An explanation of how the result fits into the origin of life, such as a proposed prebiotic setting, is usually a hypothesis.
What the paper does not address, or names as a limitation, often marks an open question.

For example, the experiment of Powner, Gerland, and Sutherland (2009) established a chemical route to activated pyrimidine nucleotides under stated laboratory conditions; whether the starting materials were available together on the early Earth is a hypothesis that the paper discusses but cannot settle by itself.
crumbs: C  How to Read a Scientific Paper

title: Appendix C — How to Read a Scientific Paper
text:
C.5 Numbers and models
Some results in this book are calculations rather than experiments: nearest-neighbour energies, melting curves, chain-length distributions and error thresholds. A calculation is only as good as its inputs. For each one, check which parameters were used, where they came from, under what conditions they were measured, and which effects the model omits. Calculations made for this book are marked as the author’s calculations, and their parameters and sources are given where they appear.




Powner, M. W., B. Gerland, and J. D. Sutherland. 2009. “Synthesis of Activated Pyrimidine Ribonucleotides in Prebiotically Plausible Conditions.” Nature 459 (7244): 239–42. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08013.
